cards.t: Chest pain: which six causes can kill, and must be excluded first?
cards.k:
Cardiac: ACS, aortic dissection, tamponade
Lung: PE, tension pneumothorax
Gut: oesophageal rupture

cards.t: Which features of chest pain raise the chance of ACS?
cards.k:
Character: pressure, exertional, eased by rest
Radiation: both arms (LR about 2.6)
Also: sweating, lasting over 20 minutes

cards.t:
Aortic dissection clues
• Which clues suggest it?
• Which test comes before any antithrombotic?
cards.k:
Clues: sudden tearing pain → back, maximal at onset
Signs: arm BP difference over 20 mmHg, pulse deficit, new AR murmur
Test: CT aortogram → before any antithrombotic

cards.t: Chest pain: what do you do in the first 10 minutes?
cards.k:
Within 10 min of first contact:
ECG → BP in both arms → IV access → troponin → chest X-ray
ST elevation → STEMI pathway
Suspected ACS → aspirin 300 mg

cards.t: How does an accelerated troponin rule-out work (ADAPT)?
cards.k:
ADAPT: troponin at 0 and 2 hours + TIMI 0 + no ischaemic ECG changes → rule-out
Faster option: 1-2 hour high-sensitivity algorithm → per your hospital
Use a validated protocol, not a guess

cards.t:
Raised troponin
• Why is it not the same as an MI?
• What is a type 2 MI?
cards.k:
Injury: troponin above the 99th percentile
MI: injury + evidence of ischaemia
Type 2 MI: supply and demand mismatch
Look at the rise and fall

cards.t: Who counts as low risk for ACS in Australia and needs no further coronary testing?
cards.k:
All of these → no further coronary testing:
Under 40, atypical symptoms, no known CAD
Normal troponin and ECG, symptom-free

cards.t: Intermediate-risk chest pain: how soon should non-invasive testing happen?
cards.k:
Intermediate risk → non-invasive testing
Ideal: within 7 days
Acceptable: up to 14 days

cards.t: What are the contraindications to a stress test?
cards.k:
Do not stress test in:
Acute MI or unstable angina
Uncontrolled arrhythmia, PE, dissection
Severe aortic stenosis
Myocarditis or pericarditis

cards.t:
Chest pain and oxygen
• When do you give oxygen?
• What is the target in COPD?
cards.k:
Oxygen only if saturations under 93%
COPD → target 88-92%

cards.t:
Non-cardiac chest pain
• Which causes are common?
• How is each treated?
cards.k:
Costochondritis → analgesia
Reflux → PPI
Pill oesophagitis → stop the pill, treat the oesophagitis
Shingles → antiviral
Biliary colic → ultrasound, LFTs
Panic → diagnosis of exclusion

cards.t:
Chest pain history
• Why can't the history rule out ACS?
• Does a GTN response prove cardiac pain?
cards.k:
History cannot rule out ACS: atypical in women, older people, diabetes
GTN relief → does not prove cardiac pain

cards.t: When must you not give GTN?
cards.k:
No GTN if:
Low BP
Inferior MI with RV involvement → do V4R
Recent PDE-5 inhibitor → sildenafil 24 hours; tadalafil longer

cards.t: What are the ECG criteria for STEMI, including the STEMI equivalents?
cards.k:
ST elevation 1 mm or more in two contiguous leads
V2-V3: 2 mm in men, 1.5 mm in women
Equivalents:
Posterior → ST depression V1-V4
aVR elevation + widespread depression
New LBBB + symptoms

cards.t:
Type 1 vs type 2 MI
• What causes each?
• How do you treat type 2?
cards.k:
Type 1: plaque rupture
Type 2: supply and demand mismatch → sepsis, fast AF, anaemia, PE
Type 2 treatment → treat the cause

cards.t:
NSTEACS: how soon should angiography happen?
• Very high risk
• High risk
• Intermediate risk
cards.k:
Very high risk → angiography within 2 hours
High risk (GRACE over 140, dynamic changes, troponin rise) → within 24 hours
Intermediate (GRACE 109-140) → within 72 hours

cards.t:
Aspirin in ACS
• What is the loading dose?
• What is the maintenance dose?
cards.k:
Load: 300 mg chewed or dissolved
Then: 100-150 mg daily

cards.t:
P2Y12 inhibitor in ACS
• Which one?
• At what doses?
• When is clopidogrel the choice?
cards.k:
Ticagrelor: 180 mg then 90 mg twice daily
Prasugrel: 60 mg then 10 mg daily → not if over 75, under 60 kg, prior stroke or TIA
Clopidogrel: 300-600 mg then 75 mg → choice with lysis or oral anticoagulation

cards.t:
ACS anticoagulation
• Which drugs?
• What must you not do?
cards.k:
Unfractionated heparin or enoxaparin (enoxaparin may be preferred)
Do not switch between them

cards.t: ACS: when do you give oxygen?
cards.k: Oxygen only if saturations under 93%

cards.t: STEMI within 12 hours: when primary PCI, when fibrinolysis?
cards.k:
Within 12 hours:
Primary PCI possible within 90 min of first medical contact → PCI
Otherwise, no contraindication → fibrinolysis

cards.t:
Lysis in STEMI
• How do you recognise failed lysis?
• What do you do?
• When is angiography after successful lysis?
cards.k:
Failed lysis: ST resolution 50% or less at 60-90 min, or unstable → transfer for rescue PCI
Successful lysis → angiography within 24 hours
(Victoria: Adult Retrieval Victoria coordinates transfer of critically ill adults and gives phone advice, 1300 36 86 61. Confirm who calls at GV Health.)

cards.t:
RV infarct
• How does it present?
• Which lead confirms it?
• How do you treat it?
cards.k:
Presents: inferior STEMI + low BP + raised JVP + clear lungs
Confirm: ST elevation in V4R
Treat: fluid; avoid GTN

cards.t:
Mechanical complications after MI
• Which ones follow?
• How does each present?
• What do you do?
cards.k:
New murmur + pulmonary oedema or shock → papillary muscle or septal rupture
Sudden tamponade → free wall rupture
Then: urgent echo → surgery

cards.t:
Low BP after angiography
• What are the causes?
• What do you do?
cards.k:
Think: bleeding (groin or retroperitoneal), re-infarction, tamponade, arrhythmia
Do: fluid → ECG → Hb → bedside echo → call cardiology

cards.t:
Pericarditis after MI
• What do you give?
• What do you avoid?
cards.k:
Give: aspirin + colchicine
Avoid: other NSAIDs early after MI

cards.t: What is the secondary prevention after MI?
cards.k:
Aspirin → indefinitely
DAPT → up to 12 months
Statin → highest tolerated (LDL under 1.8)
Beta-blocker → if EF 40% or less
ACE inhibitor → where indicated
Cardiac rehab → for all

cards.t:
ACS in a patient with AF
• Which antiplatelet goes with the anticoagulant?
• How long is triple therapy?
cards.k:
Antiplatelet → clopidogrel, with the oral anticoagulant
Triple therapy → keep it short

cards.t:
Pericarditis: cause
• What is the commonest cause?
• What is its usual course?
cards.k:
Cause: viral (coxsackie B)
Course: usually self-limiting

cards.t: Pericarditis: what are the four diagnostic criteria (two needed)?
cards.k:
Two of four:
Pleuritic pain, better leaning forward
Friction rub
Widespread concave ST elevation + PR depression
New or worse effusion
(ESC criteria)

cards.t:
ECG: pericarditis vs STEMI
• How do you tell them apart?
• What if in doubt?
cards.k:
Pericarditis: widespread, concave, PR depression, reciprocal change only in aVR
STEMI: territorial, reciprocal depression, Q waves
In doubt → treat as STEMI

cards.t: What are the four ECG stages of pericarditis?
cards.k:
1 → ST elevation
2 → back to baseline in about a week
3 → T inversion
4 → normal over weeks to months

cards.t: Pericarditis: which high-risk features mean admission?
cards.k:
Admit if any:
Fever, high white cells
Effusion over 2 cm, tamponade signs
Raised troponin
Immunocompromised, anticoagulated, trauma
NSAID failure

cards.t:
Pericarditis: NSAID
• Which NSAID?
• What dose?
• How long?
• When aspirin instead?
cards.k:
Ibuprofen with food at the lowest effective dose
Australian review: 400 mg three times daily; US page: 600-800 mg
Taper once symptoms and CRP settle
After MI or with CAD → aspirin instead

cards.t:
Pericarditis: colchicine
• What dose?
• For how long?
• What does it do?
cards.k:
0.5 mg twice daily for 3 months
Australian tablets are 0.5 mg → once daily if under 70 kg
Effect: halves recurrence

cards.t: Pericarditis on NSAIDs: who needs PPI cover?
cards.k:
PPI cover if:
Over 65, previous ulcer
On aspirin, steroids or anticoagulants

cards.t:
Pericarditis: steroids
• When are they used?
• What is their downside?
• When never?
cards.k:
Second line: NSAID failure or contraindication, autoimmune, uraemic
Downside: increase recurrence
Never in bacterial pericarditis

cards.t:
Early post-MI pericarditis
• What do you give?
• What do you avoid?
cards.k:
Give: aspirin + colchicine
Avoid: other NSAIDs and steroids early after MI

cards.t:
Dressler syndrome
• What is it?
• When does it occur?
cards.k:
Autoimmune pericarditis
Weeks to months after MI or cardiac surgery

cards.t:
After pericarditis
• When can they return to exercise?
• When can they return to competitive sport?
cards.k:
No strenuous exercise until symptoms resolve and ECG and CRP normalise
Competitive athletes → at least 3 months

cards.t:
Aortic dissection
• How does it present?
• What are the can't-miss signs?
cards.k:
Tearing chest or back pain
Aortic regurgitation murmur
Pulse deficit
Arm BP difference over 20 mmHg

cards.t:
Aortic dissection risk factors
• What are the risk factors?
• What do you think of under 40?
cards.k:
Hypertension (about 70%)
Under 40 → think Marfan, connective tissue disease, bicuspid valve
Also: smoking, family history

cards.t:
Type A vs type B dissection
• What is involved in each?
• What does each need?
cards.k:
Type A: involves ascending aorta → urgent surgical repair
Type B: descending only → usually medical; TEVAR if complicated

cards.t: Aortic dissection: what is the first-hour work-up?
cards.k:
Telemetry
Bloods: FBC, UEC, coags, troponin, D-dimer, group and hold
Tests: ECG, CXR, CT aortogram, echo
Serial BP in both arms; consider an arterial line

cards.t:
Aortic dissection test
• Which test is best?
• What can D-dimer, CXR and ECG not do?
cards.k:
Best test: CTA (most sensitive and specific)
D-dimer: high negative predictive value, cannot fully rule it out
CXR: widened mediastinum in about a third
ECG: often normal

cards.t:
Aortic dissection: who to call
• Who do you call?
• When do you involve haematology?
cards.k:
Call: cardiothoracic surgery urgently
Haematology early if on anticoagulation → reversal may be needed
(Victoria: Adult Retrieval Victoria coordinates transfer of critically ill adults and gives phone advice, 1300 36 86 61. Confirm who calls at GV Health.)

cards.t: Aortic dissection: how do you control the pain?
cards.k:
IV morphine
The page gives no dose → use your protocol

cards.t:
Aortic dissection: BP and HR
• What HR and BP targets?
• Which drug first?
• What must you never do?
cards.k:
Targets: HR under 60, SBP 100-120
First: IV labetalol or esmolol
SBP still over 120 → add nitroprusside or nicardipine
Never a vasodilator without a beta-blocker → reflex tachycardia raises wall stress

cards.t:
Low BP in aortic dissection
• What do you give?
• What do you avoid?
• What do you think of?
cards.k:
Give: fluids + noradrenaline
Avoid: inotropes
Think: tamponade

cards.t: What are the complications of type A dissection?
cards.k:
Coronaries → MI
Aortic valve → regurgitation
Carotids → stroke
Tamponade

cards.t:
Complicated type B dissection
• Which branch vessels are affected?
• How does each present?
• What is needed?
cards.k:
Renal → oliguria, failure
Mesenteric (celiac) → gut ischaemia
Spinal → leg weakness, paraplegia
Distal occlusion (Leriche)
All need TEVAR

cards.t: After aortic dissection: what are the discharge and long-term measures?
cards.k:
Statin, beta-blocker, low-dose aspirin
Stop smoking, control BP, avoid straining

cards.t:
Aortic aneurysm
• What size or growth means surgery?
• How is it different in women?
cards.k:
Surgery if: over 5.5 cm, or growth over 0.5 cm in 6 months, or over 1 cm in a year
Women: lower threshold (4.5-5 cm, debated)

cards.t:
Aortic dissection: mortality
• Type A with surgery
• Type A without surgery
• Type B
cards.k:
Type A: surgery 26% mortality vs over 50% medical (IRAD 2000)
Type B: 9% in hospital, 20% at 5 years

cards.t:
PE risk factors
• Which are strong, moderate and weak?
• What is Virchow's triad?
cards.k:
Strong (OR over 10): fracture or major surgery
Moderate (OR 2-9): OCP, hospitalised, previous VTE, cancer, sepsis
Weak (OR under 2): bed rest, long travel, age, obesity, smoking, cirrhosis, CKD
Virchow: stasis, vessel injury, hypercoagulability

cards.t:
Massive PE
• Why does the heart fail?
• Which arrest does it cause?
cards.k:
RV pressure rises → cardiac output falls → SVR rises
Septum bows into the LV → cuts filling further
Common cause of PEA arrest

cards.t:
PE rule-out
• How do PERC, D-dimer and imaging fit by probability?
• What are the D-dimer cut-offs?
cards.k:
Low probability → PERC or D-dimer
Moderate or high → imaging
D-dimer under 500 with moderate probability, or under 1000 with low probability → rules out
Age-adjusted cut-off: age x 10

cards.t:
PE: ECG
• What does the ECG show?
• How often?
cards.k:
Normal in 20%
Tachycardia is commonest (28%)
T-wave inversion V1-V4
S1Q3T3 (about 8%), new RBBB
ST elevation in aVR

cards.t:
PE: signs of RV strain
• On echo
• On CT
• On bloods
cards.k:
Echo: enlarged RV, moderate or severe TR, McConnell's sign, flat septum
CT: RV/LV over 0.9
Bloods: troponin up, NT-proBNP over 500

cards.t:
PE risk classes
• What are the three classes?
• What defines each?
cards.k:
High: arrest or SBP under 90 not from another cause (PESI IV+)
Intermediate: RV strain or troponin, no hypotension → high if both, low if only one
Low: neither

cards.t:
PE: treatment
• Which anticoagulant first?
• When do you thrombolyse?
• What does heparin actually do?
cards.k:
First: LMWH if stable with normal kidneys; otherwise UFH bolus + infusion
Thrombolysis only if high risk
Heparin stops new clot → the body dissolves the old clot

cards.t:
Massive PE with hypoxia
• Why use high-flow nasal oxygen?
• What is its limit?
cards.k:
Patient keeps breathing on their own → no positive-pressure breaths, no sedation
Treats low oxygen without the three hits
Only buys time → reperfusion is the fix

cards.t:
Massive PE
• How do you handle fluids?
• How do you handle oxygen delivery?
• How do you handle intubation, including the drugs?
cards.k:
Fluids: avoid big boluses (about 500 mL at most if hypotensive) → overstretch the RV
Intubation: avoid if you can → positive-pressure breaths and sedatives cut blood returning to the RV, BP drops, failing RV can collapse
Instead: high-flow nasal oxygen
If you must intubate: most experienced operator → ketamine → vasopressor (adrenaline or noradrenaline) ready first
(Point of Care page; the drug choices are US teaching, not verified against an Australian source.)

cards.t:
Crashing PE (shock or arrest)
• Who do you call?
• What are the treatment options?
cards.k:
Call the PE response team
Adrenaline (epinephrine)
Consider pulmonary vasodilators (NO or epoprostenol), thrombolysis or thrombectomy, think ECMO
Pads and crash cart nearby
(Point of Care page; the drug choices are US teaching, not verified against an Australian source.)
(Victoria: Adult Retrieval Victoria coordinates transfer of critically ill adults and gives phone advice, 1300 36 86 61. Confirm who calls at GV Health.)

cards.t:
Crashing PE
• What is the RV spiral?
• What can a vasopressor do and not do?
• What do inhaled pulmonary vasodilators add?
cards.k:
The spiral: clot raises RV load → RV fails → less blood to left heart → BP falls → low BP starves the RV of its own coronary flow → fails further
Vasopressor or inotrope (Australian ICU teaching: noradrenaline or adrenaline, or milrinone) → raises the BP that feeds the RV → buys time, does not shift the clot
Fix: reperfusion (thrombolysis, catheter treatment or surgery, via the PE response team)
Inhaled nitric oxide → relaxes only lung vessels → lowers RV load without dropping the BP → ICU decision, not an RMO one
Which pressor first: per your hospital protocol
(Checked against LITFL, written by an Alfred ICU intensivist, and the Canberra Hospital PE response pathway; corrected from the pasted note, which put adrenaline first.)

cards.t: What are the absolute contraindications to tPA (strokes, surgery, trauma, bleeding)?
cards.k:
Haemorrhagic stroke
Ischaemic stroke in the last 3 months
AVM
Recent brain or spine surgery
Head trauma with fracture or brain injury in 3 weeks
Serious active bleeding

cards.t: What are the relative contraindications to tPA?
cards.k:
CNS tumour
Major surgery in 2-3 weeks
Platelets under 100, INR over 1.7, fibrinogen under 150
Oral anticoagulant
BP over 180/110, age over 75
Advanced cirrhosis

cards.t: What did PEITHO show about thrombolysis in intermediate-risk PE, and when do you lyse?
cards.k:
PEITHO, intermediate-risk PE: no long-term benefit → more major bleeding and haemorrhagic stroke
Lyse in massive PE → to prevent immediate death

cards.t:
PE special situations
• Cancer
• Malabsorption or obesity
• Subsegmental PE
• Negative leg Doppler
cards.k:
Cancer → LMWH beats warfarin (CLOT)
Malabsorption or BMI over 40 → DOACs less reliable
Subsegmental PE, low recurrence risk → no anticoagulation
Negative leg Doppler → does not rule out PE

cards.t: Massive PE: why can intubation kill (the three hits)?
cards.k:
Three hits at once:
Positive-pressure breaths → cut blood returning to the RV
Inflated lungs → raise the load on the RV
Induction drugs → lower the BP that feeds it
The failing RV spirals
(Standard teaching, explained in The right heart, simply.)

cards.t:
PE: apixaban and duration
• What apixaban dosing?
• How long do you treat provoked PE?
• How long for unprovoked PE?
• How long for cancer PE?
cards.k:
Dose: apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days → then 5 mg twice daily
Provoked → 3 months
Unprovoked with low bleeding risk → indefinite
Cancer → indefinite

cards.t:
Unprovoked PE
• What is the recurrence risk?
• Which follow-up tests do you do, and not do?
cards.k:
Recurrence off treatment: about 10% in year 1 → then 5% a year
Do: age-appropriate cancer screening
Do not: thrombophilia testing in the acute phase (exception: high concern for antiphospholipid syndrome)

cards.t: Tamponade: why does the speed of fluid collection matter more than its size?
cards.k:
Speed matters more than size
Small effusion that collects fast (after a procedure) → can cause tamponade
Large effusion that collects slowly → may not

cards.t:
Tamponade signs
• Which signs are most useful?
• Which are late?
cards.k:
Useful: breathlessness, tachycardia, raised JVP, pulsus paradoxus over 10 mmHg
Late and insensitive: low BP, Beck triad

cards.t:
Pulsus paradoxus
• How do you measure it with a cuff?
• What value is significant?
cards.k:
Cuff up → pressure where sounds appear only in expiration
minus pressure where heard throughout
Over 10 mmHg → pulsus paradoxus
Under 10 mmHg → tamponade very unlikely

cards.t:
Tamponade tests
• What does the ECG show?
• What does the chest X-ray show?
cards.k:
ECG: electrical alternans (16-21%), low voltage
X-ray: big globular heart

cards.t: What are the echo signs of tamponade?
cards.k:
Effusion
RV diastolic collapse
RA systolic collapse
Plethoric IVC
Swinging heart

cards.t: What are the causes of pericardial effusion?
cards.k:
Procedures, pericarditis
Cancer: lung, breast, lymphoma
Uraemia, hypothyroidism
Autoimmune, radiation, blood

cards.t: Which tests do you send on pericardial fluid?
cards.k:
Cell count, protein, LDH
Gram stain and culture
TB tests, cytology

cards.t: What is the definitive treatment for tamponade?
cards.k:
Pericardiocentesis
Do not delay it in an unstable patient

cards.t:
Tamponade: what to avoid
• Which treatments must you avoid, and why?
• Why is intubation risky?
cards.k:
Avoid: diuretics, vasodilators
Avoid intubation if at all possible → positive pressure lowers venous return

cards.t: Haemopericardium from dissection, free wall rupture or trauma: who fixes it?
cards.k:
Dissection, free wall rupture or trauma → cardiothoracic surgery
Not just a needle
(Victoria: Adult Retrieval Victoria coordinates transfer of critically ill adults and gives phone advice, 1300 36 86 61. Confirm who calls at GV Health.)

cards.t:
After cardiac surgery
• What suggests clot tamponade?
• What do you do?
cards.k:
Drains suddenly stop + BP falls + CVP rises → clot tamponade
Call the surgeon → re-opening may be needed

cards.t:
New AF
• Which triggers do you look for?
• Which bloods do you send?
cards.k:
Look for: thyroid, alcohol, sepsis, ischaemia, valve disease
Also: low K or Mg, PE, heart failure, recent surgery
Send: TFTs, electrolytes with K and Mg, troponin, creatinine
The creatinine now also decides the anticoagulant dose

cards.t: What are the CHA2DS2-VASc points?
cards.k:
Heart failure 1
Hypertension 1
Age 75+ 2
Diabetes 1
Stroke or TIA 2
Vascular disease 1
Age 65-74 1
Female 1

cards.t: AF: who gets anticoagulated (CHA2DS2-VASc cut-offs)?
cards.k:
CHA2DS2-VASc 2 or more in men
CHA2DS2-VASc 3 or more in women
(stroke risk 2% a year or more)

cards.t:
AF and bleeding risk
• Should a bleeding score stop anticoagulation?
• Which modifiable bleeding risks do you fix?
cards.k:
Do not use a bleeding score (HAS-BLED) to withhold anticoagulation
Fix the modifiable risks: uncontrolled hypertension, alcohol, NSAIDs, antiplatelets, anaemia, labile INR

cards.t:
AF rate control
• What heart-rate target, and with LV dysfunction?
• Which first-line drugs?
• Which drug to avoid?
cards.k:
Target: under 110 (under 80 if LV dysfunction or symptoms)
First line: beta-blocker or diltiazem/verapamil
Avoid: non-dihydropyridine CCB with moderate or severe LV systolic dysfunction

cards.t:
AF: second-line rate control
• What is second-line rate control?
• What do you do in pre-excited AF (WPW), stable?
• What do you do in pre-excited AF (WPW), unstable?
cards.k:
Ordinary AF: digoxin (slow, about 2 hours) or amiodarone as backup
Pre-excited AF (WPW): no AV-nodal blockers, avoid IV amiodarone too
Unstable → synchronised shock
Stable → procainamide (RACGP); availability in your hospital not confirmed, follow your protocol

cards.t: AF: who benefits from rhythm control?
cards.k:
Symptomatic despite rate control
First episode
Heart failure (especially HFrEF)
Young, athletes
Patient preference

cards.t:
Can this AF be cardioverted now?
• If unstable
• If stable under 48 hours
• If stable over 48 hours
cards.k:
Unstable → shock now; do not wait for a TOE or anticoagulation
Stable, under 48 hours → cardioversion can proceed (with mild symptoms, rate control and watching is also fine)
Stable, over 48 hours or unknown → exclude left atrial thrombus with TOE first, or anticoagulate for weeks (ANZCOR 11.9)

cards.t:
Electrical cardioversion of AF
• How do you do it?
• At how many joules?
• What must you never do?
cards.k:
Sedate → anteroposterior pads → synchronise to the QRS → start about 100 J biphasic
Never defibrillate AF

cards.t:
Drug cardioversion of AF
• When can you use flecainide?
• What do you use otherwise?
• Why the split?
cards.k:
Not a sequence: the heart decides
No structural heart disease → flecainide (oral or IV) can be considered, with an AV-nodal blocker given first
LV systolic dysfunction, moderate LVH or coronary artery disease → no flecainide → amiodarone
Why: class Ic drugs can trigger fatal ventricular arrhythmias in a scarred or failing heart
(2018 Australian AF guideline: flecainide or amiodarone are the recommended drugs. It does not name propafenone, dofetilide or ibutilide, and I could not confirm they are used in Australia.)

cards.t:
Flecainide and AV-nodal blockers
• Why give an AV-nodal blocker before flecainide?
• How does 1 to 1 flutter happen?
• When must you not give the blocker?
cards.k:
Flecainide slows the atria → AF can organise into flutter, and flutter slows from about 300 to about 220 a minute
At 300 the AV node blocks every second beat → 2 to 1 → ventricles about 150
At 220 the AV node can pass every beat → 1 to 1 → ventricles about 220 → dangerous
So: give an AV-nodal blocker first (beta-blocker, or diltiazem or verapamil) (2018 Australian AF guideline)
Only in ordinary AF or flutter → in pre-excited AF (WPW) give no AV-nodal blocker: it sends impulses down the accessory pathway, which has no rate limit → VF
Pre-excited AF: electrical cardioversion is the safe default
(Your note named procainamide and ibutilide for pre-excited AF; I could not confirm either is used in Australia, so they are left out.)

cards.t:
Pre-excited AF
• Why are AV-nodal blockers dangerous?
• Which drugs do you avoid?
• What if unstable?
cards.k:
AV node has a speed limiter; the accessory pathway (delta wave) does not
Blocking the node → fast atrial rate goes down the accessory pathway → ventricles can go dangerously fast
Avoid: beta-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin
Unstable → synchronised shock

cards.t:
AF: anticoagulant choice
• Which anticoagulant first line?
• When warfarin instead (valves and kidneys)?
• Why not a DOAC there?
cards.k:
First line: DOAC (apixaban, dabigatran, rivaroxaban) for non-valvular AF (2018 Australian AF guideline)
Non-valvular here means no moderate to severe mitral stenosis and no mechanical valve → mild mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation and aortic valve disease can still take a DOAC
Warfarin (INR 2-3) → mechanical valve, or moderate to severe mitral stenosis
Why mechanical valve: the metal surface switches on clotting strongly → in RE-ALIGN, dabigatran gave more clots and more bleeding than warfarin
Why mitral stenosis: blood pools in a large left atrium → in INVICTUS (rheumatic heart disease), warfarin prevented more strokes and deaths than rivaroxaban
Kidneys (Australian product information, per NPS): apixaban not below CrCl 25, dabigatran not below 30, rivaroxaban 15 mg with caution at 15-29 → below these, warfarin
Dialysis: anticoagulation is debated; warfarin only if used (2018 Australian AF guideline)
Aspirin alone is not enough
(Corrected from your note: in Australia apixaban is not used below CrCl 25, so it is not the alternative at CrCl under 15. INR 2-3 is standard teaching. The trial names are from your note; I did not re-read the trials.)

cards.t: AF with cirrhosis: can you use a DOAC (Australian apixaban product information)?
cards.k:
DOACs are contraindicated in cirrhosis
Australian apixaban product information: contraindicated in liver disease with coagulopathy and clinically relevant bleeding risk, including severe (Child-Pugh C); caution in mild or moderate
Check the product information for rivaroxaban and dabigatran

cards.t:
DOACs for AF in Australia
• What are the doses and dose reductions?
• How do you remember which are once or twice daily?
cards.k:
Twice daily: apixaban and dabigatran ('Always Double'). Once daily: rivaroxaban and edoxaban ('Really Easy')
Apixaban 5 mg twice daily → 2.5 mg twice daily if two of: age 80+, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 umol/L or more
Rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily with food → 15 mg if CrCl 30-49 (15-29: 15 mg with caution)
Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily → 110 mg twice daily in the groups the product information lists (such as older age or high bleeding risk); not below CrCl 30
Edoxaban 60 → 30 mg: not one of the three DOACs NPS lists as approved in Australia
Check Australian product information
(Corrected from your note: the Australian rivaroxaban 15 mg dose is for CrCl 30-49, with caution at 15-29, not 15-49. Your dabigatran 110 mg list (age 80+, verapamil, age 75-79, CrCl 30-50) is not verified against the Australian product information; check it.)

cards.t:
AF after PCI
• What antithrombotics?
• For how long?
• What at 12 months?
cards.k:
Why: stent needs antiplatelets, AF needs an anticoagulant, all three raise bleeding a lot
So: stop aspirin early (US page 1-4 weeks; Australian review about 1 month)
Keep: anticoagulant + P2Y12 inhibitor
Clopidogrel preferred over ticagrelor or prasugrel; DOAC preferred over warfarin
At 12 months → stop the antiplatelet, keep the anticoagulant alone
(NHFA/CSANZ 2018 via Medicine Today 2019; check eTG)

cards.t: Which drugs keep sinus rhythm in AF, and what are the cautions?
cards.k:
Class Ic → avoid in CAD or structural disease
Amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide, dronedarone
Advanced conduction disease → no antiarrhythmic without pacing

cards.t:
AF catheter ablation
• What is done?
• Who does best?
• What about anticoagulation after?
cards.k:
Pulmonary vein isolation
Works best: paroxysmal AF (70-80%), heart failure, young symptomatic patients
Anticoagulation after → based on the score, not the rhythm

cards.t: AF: which risk factors do you modify, and with what targets?
cards.k:
Weight loss 10% or more
Exercise 210 minutes a week
BP under 130/80
Treat sleep apnoea
Alcohol under 3 drinks a week
Stop smoking, glycaemic control
Caffeine restriction not advised

cards.t:
AF burden
• How long an episode carries stroke risk?
• When is risk highest?
cards.k:
Episodes over 17-24 hours → significant risk
Over twofold risk from 1 hour
Risk highest in the 5 days after an episode

cards.t:
Bradycardia
• What rate defines it?
• When do symptoms start?
• What are sick sinus, junctional and physiological bradycardia?
cards.k:
Bradycardia: under 60, but symptoms usually start under 50
Sick sinus syndrome: SA node dysfunction
Junctional rhythm: starts in the AV node
Athletes and sleep: can be physiological

cards.t:
Heart blocks
• What are the four heart blocks?
• How does the PR behave in each?
cards.k:
First degree: long fixed PR
Mobitz I: PR lengthens → then a drop
Mobitz II: fixed PR → sudden drops
Complete: atria and ventricles independent

cards.t:
Complete heart block
• What sets the beat?
• How do junctional and ventricular escape differ?
cards.k:
Nothing gets through → a backup pacemaker below the block sets the beat
Higher backup = better
Block at the AV node → junctional escape: 40-60 a minute, narrow QRS, steadier
Block in the wires below → ventricular escape: 20-40 a minute, wide QRS, unreliable (LITFL)

cards.t: Bradycardia: which adverse signs make the patient unstable?
cards.k:
Systolic BP under 90
Heart rate under 40
Ventricular arrhythmia
Heart failure
(US page also lists: confusion, chest pain, breathlessness)

cards.t: Which bradycardia findings mark asystole risk, and what do you do even if the patient looks well?
cards.k:
Marks asystole risk:
Recent asystole, Mobitz II
Complete block with broad QRS or rate under 40
Pause over 3 seconds
→ pads on + call cardiology, even if the patient looks well

cards.t: Bradycardia: what is the first-hour work-up?
cards.k:
Telemetry, 12-lead ECG
FBC, UEC (with potassium), TSH, troponin
Echo
Check: prior ECGs, drug chart, prior heart disease

cards.t: Bradycardia: what are the four can't-miss causes?
cards.k:
ACS (especially inferior MI)
Complete heart block
Beta-blocker or calcium-channel blocker toxicity
Hyperkalaemia

cards.t: Bradycardia: which reversible causes do you look for?
cards.k:
Drugs: beta-blockers, CCBs, amiodarone, opioids, SSRIs
Hyperkalaemia, hypothyroidism, hypothermia
Raised intracranial pressure
Infection (Lyme, endocarditis)
Ischaemia, vagal tone

cards.t:
Atropine for bradycardia
• What dose in Australia?
• How often?
• Up to what maximum?
• Why not too low?
cards.k:
Australia: 500-600 mcg IV every 3-5 minutes → up to 3 mg
US page: 1 mg a dose
Too low a dose can slow the heart further

cards.t:
If atropine fails
• What adrenaline infusion?
• How do you pace?
• How do you confirm capture?
cards.k:
Adrenaline infusion: 2-10 mcg/min
Or pacing: transcutaneous at 70-80 a minute, start near 30 mA → until capture
Capture = QRS after every spike + a pulse
Chest twitching proves nothing

cards.t:
Beta-blocker or calcium-channel blocker toxicity
• What do you give?
• Who do you call?
cards.k:
Glucagon
Or insulin with glucose and potassium
Much higher adrenaline doses
Call: Poisons Information Centre 13 11 26
The glucagon dose is not in the Australian source → use toxicology guidance

cards.t: When will atropine not work?
cards.k:
Atropine fails in:
Complete heart block (especially wide QRS)
Block below the AV node
Transplanted heart
The page also warns about acute MI

cards.t:
Block at the AV node vs below it
• Why does each behave differently?
• What does atropine do?
cards.k:
Block at the AV node: node tires gradually → slow cells need time to reset → each early signal passes more slowly → warning signs; atropine helps
Block below (the wires): fast and all-or-none → conduct or fail suddenly → no warning; atropine fails and can make it worse
See the Heart block pages in this app

cards.t:
Atropine in a block below the AV node
• Why can it make the block worse?
• What would you see on the monitor?
cards.k:
Atropine speeds the sinus node and AV node, not the wires below
More impulses reach a diseased infranodal wire → it cannot recover in time → more beats are blocked
Seen: block worsens, e.g. 1:1 becomes 2:1, heart rate falls (70 → 40)
→ Do not keep repeating atropine: move to adrenaline infusion or pacing
(Study Kit, Heart block: node or below? Australian source not found; standard teaching.)

cards.t: What are the indications for a permanent pacemaker?
cards.k:
Symptomatic sinus bradycardia (with or without pauses)
Complete heart block
Symptomatic second-degree block
Syncope from bradycardia
Correct reversible causes first → involve EP

cards.t:
Tachycardia
• Which adverse signs mean unstable?
• What is the treatment?
cards.k:
Adverse signs: systolic BP under 90, heart rate over 150, chest pain, heart failure, drowsy or confused
Unstable → synchronised cardioversion with sedation

cards.t: Tachycardia: what goes in each of the four boxes (narrow or wide, regular or irregular)?
cards.k:
Narrow regular → sinus, flutter, AVNRT/AVRT
Narrow irregular → AF, MAT
Wide regular → VT
Wide irregular → AF with block, pre-excited AF, torsades

cards.t:
Sinus tachycardia
• What are the causes?
• How do you treat it?
cards.k:
A sign, not a rhythm to treat
Causes: pain, anxiety, bleeding or hypovolaemia, fever or sepsis, hypoxia, PE, heart failure, ACS, alcohol withdrawal, thyroid, caffeine, drugs
Find and treat the cause
Never shock it or slow it with drugs

cards.t: Tachycardia: what do you do in the first minute at the bedside?
cards.k:
Oxygen if low → monitor → IV → pads → 12-lead ECG
Bloods: K, Mg, troponin, lactate, TSH
Call your senior
No pulse → arrest algorithm

cards.t: Narrow regular tachycardia, stable: what is the treatment sequence and doses?
cards.k:
Valsalva
→ adenosine 6 mg
→ adenosine 12 mg (flush at least 20 mL)
→ verapamil 2.5-5 mg or diltiazem 15-20 mg if adenosine is unsuitable

cards.t:
Modified Valsalva
• How do you do it?
• How well does it work?
cards.k:
Strain into a 10 mL syringe for 15 seconds
→ lie flat, legs raised 45 degrees, for 15 seconds
Converts about 43% (standard Valsalva 5-20%)

cards.t:
Narrow irregular tachycardia (AF), stable
• Which drugs and doses?
• When can you not cardiovert?
cards.k:
Metoprolol 5 mg IV (not with wheeze or decompensated heart failure)
Or digoxin 250-500 mcg
Over 48 hours → no cardioversion unless anticoagulated or TOE clear

cards.t:
Wide regular tachycardia
• What do you treat it as?
• Which drug and dose?
• What must you never give?
cards.k:
Treat it as VT
Amiodarone 300 mg over 20-60 minutes → then 900 mg over 24 hours
Never verapamil or diltiazem

cards.t:
Torsades
• What do you stop?
• What do you correct and give (magnesium dose)?
• What do you avoid?
• What if unstable?
cards.k:
Stop QT drugs
Correct potassium
Magnesium 5 mmol IV over 10 minutes (may repeat once) → then 20 mmol over 4 hours
Avoid amiodarone
Adverse signs (shock) → unstable
The US page's '2-4 mg' looks like a typo for grams

cards.t:
Tachycardia: shock fails
• What do you give?
• What do you do then?
cards.k:
Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 10-20 minutes
→ repeat the shock
→ then 900 mg over 24 hours

cards.t:
Sedation for cardioversion
• What does the US page suggest?
• What does ANZCOR say?
cards.k:
US page: fentanyl 50 mcg + midazolam 1-2 mg
ANZCOR: names no drug or dose
→ use your protocol and senior or anaesthetic help

cards.t:
Respiratory support ladder
• What is the ladder?
• When BiPAP vs CPAP?
cards.k:
Non-rebreather → HFNC → NIPPV → intubate
NIPPV: BiPAP for COPD, CPAP for heart failure
Watch PaCO2 and pH

cards.t:
Pre-excited AF
• Which drugs do you avoid?
• What is safest?
• What if you can't tell it from VT?
cards.k:
Avoid: adenosine, digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem
Safest: electrical cardioversion (usually)
Cannot tell it from VT → treat the same way: pads on, 12-lead ECG, call your senior early
Unstable → synchronised shock

cards.t:
ADHF: what do you do for each profile?
• Warm-wet
• Warm-dry
• Cold-wet
• Cold-dry
cards.k:
Warm + wet → IV diuretic (most common)
Warm + dry → look for another cause
Cold + wet → shock → ICU
Cold + dry → senior review, stop diuretics, consider cautious fluid

cards.t:
Cardiogenic shock
• How do you spot it?
• What do you do straight away?
cards.k:
Spot it: systolic under 90 for over 30 min, cold and clammy, narrow pulse pressure, confusion, rising lactate, poor urine
Straight away: call senior and ICU → stop the beta-blocker and vasodilators
(Victoria: Adult Retrieval Victoria coordinates transfer of critically ill adults and gives phone advice, 1300 36 86 61. Confirm who calls at GV Health.)

cards.t:
ADHF: NT-proBNP and findings
• What NT-proBNP rules it out?
• Which exam and X-ray findings are most useful?
cards.k:
NT-proBNP under 300 → ADHF unlikely
Best signs: S3 (LR 11), JVP (LR 5)
Crackles are not specific
CXR oedema → LR 12

cards.t: What are the common triggers of decompensated heart failure?
cards.k:
Salt, fluid, missed tablets
Ischaemia, arrhythmia (AF), hypertension
Drugs: NSAIDs, steroids, verapamil or diltiazem
Infection, kidney injury
Alcohol or cocaine, valve disease
Iatrogenic IV fluid

cards.t:
Acute pulmonary oedema
• What are the first steps?
• What do you avoid?
cards.k:
Sit up → oxygen if hypoxic
CPAP or NIV if oxygen not enough or CO2 rises
GTN if BP allows → infusion from about 5-10 mcg/min
IV furosemide
Avoid morphine

cards.t: ADHF: what starting dose of IV loop diuretic?
cards.k:
About twice the home oral dose, given IV (higher with kidney disease)
Australian ED handbook: furosemide 80 mg IV, or the usual dose IV

cards.t:
After the first IV diuretic dose
• What do you check at 1 hour?
• What do you check at 3-4 hours?
• What do you do?
cards.k:
1 hour: urine → none, check for shock and double the dose
3-4 hours: less than halfway to goal → double; otherwise repeat
Second dose by early afternoon

cards.t:
HFrEF
• What are the four pillars?
• When do you start them?
cards.k:
ARNI preferred → or ACE inhibitor (36-hour washout before ARNI); ARB last-line
Beta-blocker → bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, nebivolol
MRA
SGLT2 inhibitor → dapagliflozin or empagliflozin
Start all as soon as clinically possible

cards.t:
Diuretic classes
• Where does each class act?
• How much sodium is taken back at each site?
cards.k:
Proximal tubule → acetazolamide (about 65% of sodium taken back)
Thick limb of the loop → loop diuretics (about 25%, the strongest)
Distal tubule → thiazides (about 5%)
Collecting duct → spironolactone (about 3-5%)
Block one part → later parts take back more
(Percentages are standard physiology, not from an Australian source.)

cards.t:
IV furosemide
• Why give it IV in congestion?
• How fast can you push it?
cards.k:
Oral: absorption unpredictable (Australian product information: mean about 60% in healthy men, wide spread) and a swollen gut absorbs less
IV: starts in about 5 min; oral about 1 hour
Steep dose-response → below a threshold dose nothing happens; kidney disease raises the threshold
IV rate: no faster than 4 mg/minute (hearing)

cards.t:
Furosemide, bumetanide and torasemide
• How long do they last?
• How do the doses compare?
• What is available in Australia?
cards.k:
Furosemide: half-life up to about 100 min (longer in kidney or liver disease) → oral lasts 6-8 hours, IV about 2 hours
Bumetanide: absorbed almost completely, half-life about 1 hour (your notes)
Dose: about 1 mg bumetanide = 40 mg oral furosemide; oral furosemide about half as potent as IV (standard teaching)
Bumetanide: registered in Australia (Burinex), not PBS-listed for heart failure
Torasemide: half-life about 3-6 hours, once daily (your notes) → could not confirm it is marketed in Australia; check your hospital

cards.t:
Thiazides in heart failure
• How strong are they?
• When do they work poorly?
• When are they used?
cards.k:
Site: distal tubule → weaker than loops, poor at low GFR
Use: add-on for diuretic resistance, not routine
Medicine Today July 2026: hydrochlorothiazide 12.5-25 mg daily; metolazone not PBS-listed for heart failure
Chlorthalidone (Hygroton): in the Australian medicines listing, availability not confirmed → check your hospital protocol

cards.t:
Creatinine rising during diuresis
• What does it usually mean?
• What do you do?
• Which two blood results tell you diuresis is going well?
cards.k:
Usually haemodynamic, not kidney damage
Less fluid in the circulation → kidney filters at slightly lower pressure → creatinine creeps up
Still congested → keep diuresing, trust the exam
Going well (sweet spot): bicarbonate rising + creatinine stable or only a little up
Why: salt water leaves → bicarbonate left behind is more concentrated (contraction alkalosis)
Worry: creatinine keeps climbing while they look dry, BP falls, or urine output drops → discuss with your senior

cards.t:
Diuretic resistance on furosemide 80 mg IV twice daily
• What are the next steps?
• Why check K before acetazolamide?
cards.k:
Not enough urine on furosemide 80 mg IV twice daily:
Call cardiology
Then: furosemide infusion, or add thiazide (metolazone), or add acetazolamide if alkalotic and K above 4 (ADVOR)
Check K first → acetazolamide wastes potassium like the loops
Not verified: the K above 4 cut-off is from the Point of Care page, not checked against the Australian Diamox product information. Confirm with your hospital protocol.

cards.t:
Holding heart failure drugs in hospital
• When do you hold or reduce ARNI, ACE inhibitor, ARB, MRA and beta-blocker?
• Why does potassium decide the first four?
cards.k:
Why potassium: ACE inhibitor, ARB and ARNI block angiotensin II → less aldosterone; MRA blocks aldosterone itself → kidney keeps potassium → K rises
ARNI, ACE inhibitor, ARB or MRA:
Caution → systolic under 95, K over 5.0, eGFR under 20
Reduce → K 5.5-6.0
Withhold → K over 6.0
Beta-blocker: caution → HR under 55 or systolic under 95
(Mechanism: RACGP AFP, Persistent hyperkalaemia.)

cards.t:
Loop diuretics
• Which electrolytes do they waste?
• What acid-base change follows?
• How do you protect against it?
cards.k:
Lose: sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium, magnesium, hydrogen
Result: low K and Mg + contraction alkalosis
They do not retain potassium or hydrogen
Protect: check K and Mg daily → replace early → keep spironolactone going to hold potassium

cards.t:
Thiazides vs spironolactone
• What does each do to potassium?
• What does each do to acid-base?
• What does each do to sodium?
cards.k:
Thiazides → lose potassium and hydrogen → low K, alkalosis
Thiazides → classic drug cause of hyponatraemia; keep calcium (useful in calcium stones)
Spironolactone → blocks aldosterone → keeps potassium and hydrogen → high K, metabolic acidosis; can add to low sodium
Spironolactone improves survival in HFrEF → check K and creatinine

cards.t:
Acetazolamide
• How does it work?
• What acid-base change does it cause?
• When is it added in heart failure?
cards.k:
Blocks carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule → loses bicarbonate and sodium → metabolic acidosis
In heart failure: add-on when loops are not enough (ADVOR), especially if alkalotic
Not a starter
Medicine Today: 250-500 mg daily

cards.t:
Diuretic resistance
• Why do diuretics stop working?
• What is the fix for each reason?
cards.k:
Braking: drug wears off, kidney grabs sodium back → doses more often or an infusion
Downstream catch-up: later segments take back more → add a second class (thiazide, spironolactone or acetazolamide)
Poor gut absorption → give IV
Poor kidney function → higher threshold dose
Acetazolamide is not the long-acting fix for braking; it is a second site of action

cards.t:
IV iron in heart failure
• What are the criteria?
• Which iron?
• Why not oral?
cards.k:
Ferritin under 100 µg/L, or 100-299 with TSAT under 20%
→ IV ferric carboxymaltose
Oral iron does not work in heart failure

cards.t: ADHF: what is the discharge plan?
cards.k:
Oral diuretic when symptoms and JVP improve → ideally tested for 24 hours
Daily weights → 2 kg change in 2 days → contact GP within 24 hours
Review within 1-2 weeks
Uptitrate the pillars at least twice before discharge

cards.t:
Heart failure devices
• How long after full medical therapy?
• Who gets an ICD or CRT?
cards.k:
After 3-6 months of full therapy:
ICD → EF under 35% (US criteria)
CRT → EF under 35% with QRS over 150 ms, especially LBBB
Cardiology decides

cards.t:
CRT
• Why does it help most when the QRS is very wide with LBBB?
• Why does it help less with RBBB?
cards.k:
LBBB → left ventricle activated late → ventricles squeeze out of step → pump wastes effort
Wider QRS → bigger delay
CRT paces the right ventricle and the late left lateral wall (lead through the coronary sinus) together → fixes that delay
RBBB or non-specific delay → late part is elsewhere or scattered → pacing the left wall helps less
Cut-offs (QRS 150 ms or more, EF 35% or less, sinus rhythm, full therapy) are on the card above; cardiology decides
(Mechanism is standard teaching; the Australian 2018 heart failure guideline could not be opened this run to confirm the exact cut-offs.)

cards.t:
Hypertensive urgency vs emergency
• What BP?
• What separates them?
cards.k:
Both: usually over 180/120
Emergency: organ damage → brain, eyes, heart, aorta, kidneys, blood
Urgency: no organ damage → mild headache allowed

cards.t:
High BP in pregnancy over 20 weeks or postpartum
• What do you assume?
• Who do you call?
cards.k:
High BP over 20 weeks or postpartum → pre-eclampsia until proven otherwise
Call obstetrics

cards.t: The ward call for high BP: what do you do?
cards.k:
See the patient → re-measure properly → look for organ damage
Treat: pain, retention, anxiety, missed tablets
Well patient → no IV drugs

cards.t: Hypertensive emergency: what is the organ-damage work-up?
cards.k:
ECG, troponin, creatinine, urinalysis
FBC and film (MAHA)
Chest X-ray, fundoscopy
CT head if neurological
CT aortogram if dissection suspected

cards.t:
Hypertensive emergency: lowering BP
• How fast do you lower it?
• Why not faster?
cards.k:
First hour: no more than 25% fall
Then about 160/100 over 2-5 hours
Then normal over days
Too fast → stroke, kidney injury

cards.t:
Hypertensive urgency
• What are the BP targets?
• What is the plan?
cards.k:
Under 160/100 over hours
Then under 130/90 over days
Oral drugs + GP follow-up

cards.t:
Hypertensive emergency: IV drugs
• Which drugs?
• What caution for each?
cards.k:
Labetalol → bolus or infusion
GTN → infusion
Hydralazine → unpredictable
Nicardipine → not stocked everywhere in Australia; check your formulary

cards.t:
Aortic dissection and BP
• Which drug first?
• What targets?
• What must you never give alone?
cards.k:
First: beta-blocker (labetalol or esmolol)
Targets within an hour: systolic under 120, heart rate under 60
Never a vasodilator alone

cards.t:
Hypertension with ACS or pulmonary oedema
• Which drug?
• What target?
• Which drug to avoid?
cards.k:
Drug: GTN
Target: systolic under 140 within an hour
Avoid beta-blockers in pulmonary oedema or shock

cards.t:
Stimulant toxicity with high BP
• What first?
• What to avoid?
• Who to call?
cards.k:
First: benzodiazepines
Avoid: a beta-blocker alone
Call: Poisons Information Centre 13 11 26

cards.t:
PRES
• What is it, and how does it present?
• Where does the MRI show change?
cards.k:
PRES presents: headache, seizures, confusion, visual loss
MRI → parieto-occipital oedema

cards.t: What are the secondary causes of hypertension?
cards.k:
Drugs: NSAIDs, steroids, pill, stimulants
Sleep apnoea
Renal artery stenosis
Primary aldosteronism, phaeochromocytoma
Thyroid, Cushing, coarctation

cards.t:
Syncope
• What is it?
• Which mimics must you exclude first?
cards.k:
Syncope: brief LOC from low brain blood flow → fast full recovery
Exclude first: hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, intoxication, seizure, stroke

cards.t:
Three kinds of syncope
• What are they?
• How common is each?
• What if unclear?
cards.k:
Reflex: about 60%
Orthostatic: 15%
Cardiac: 15%
If reflex or orthostatic is not clear → think cardiac

cards.t:
Seizure vs syncope
• Which feature points to seizure?
• Which features don't help?
cards.k:
Points to seizure: prolonged confusion afterwards
Does not help: tongue biting and incontinence (occur in both)

cards.t: What are the red flags for cardiac syncope (including the family history)?
cards.k:
Exertional or supine, no warning
Palpitations, chest pain, breathlessness
Heart disease, abnormal ECG
Family history of sudden death

cards.t: What are the can't-miss causes of syncope?
cards.k:
Arrhythmia, aortic stenosis, PE
Bleeding: GI bleed, ruptured AAA, ectopic pregnancy
Seizure, stroke

cards.t: Syncope: what do you look for on the ECG?
cards.k:
Heart block or pauses
Long QT, delta wave (WPW)
Brugada, HCM voltages, ARVC epsilon wave
Ischaemia, new arrhythmia

cards.t:
Lying and standing BP
• How do you do it?
• What fall is orthostatic hypotension?
cards.k:
Measure: lying → immediately on standing → at 3 minutes
Orthostatic hypotension: fall of 20 systolic or 10 diastolic

cards.t: Syncope: which tests does everyone get?
cards.k:
Everyone: ECG, glucose, FBC, electrolytes, troponin
Admitted → telemetry
Women of child-bearing age → pregnancy test

cards.t:
Syncope: tests
• When do you order an echo?
• When do you order a CT head?
• Is carotid Doppler useful?
cards.k:
Echo → murmur, heart disease or abnormal ECG
CT head → head strike with anticoagulants, or focal signs
Carotid Doppler → rarely helps

cards.t: What are the causes of orthostatic hypotension?
cards.k:
Drugs: diuretics, vasodilators, alpha-blockers, beta-blockers
Dehydration
Autonomic failure: Parkinson disease, diabetes, amyloid

cards.t:
Treating syncope: how do you treat each kind?
• Reflex
• Orthostatic
• Cardiac
cards.k:
Reflex → education, counter-pressure
Orthostatic → stop culprit drugs, fluids, stockings → midodrine or fludrocortisone by specialist
Cardiac → treat the cause

cards.t: Syncope and private driving (Austroads): what are the rules?
cards.k:
Typical vasovagal, unlikely while driving → fit
Single blackout, uncertain cause → 6 months
Two or more, over 24 hours apart → 12 months
Licensing authority decides (Austroads)

cards.t:
Respiratory distress
• What do you look at first?
• What do you do straight away?
cards.k:
Look: talking? rate, effort, SpO2, pulse, BP, drowsiness
Do: sit up → monitor → IV access → call for help early

cards.t:
Oxygen targets
• What are the targets for most adults?
• What are the targets for CO2 retainers?
• When is oxygen not needed?
cards.k:
Most acutely unwell adults: 92 to 96%
COPD or CO2 retainers: 88 to 92% (TSANZ)
No oxygen for breathlessness without hypoxia

cards.t:
Stridor or facial swelling
• What do you give?
• Who do you call?
cards.k:
Upper airway obstruction or anaphylaxis
→ IM adrenaline + call anaesthetics early

cards.t:
Tension pneumothorax
• How do you diagnose it?
• Do you wait for imaging?
cards.k:
Breathless + absent air entry one side + low BP + high airway pressures
→ decompress without waiting for imaging

cards.t:
Reading a gas
• Type 1 vs type 2 failure
• Acute vs chronic
cards.k:
Type 1: low O2, normal or low CO2
Type 2: high CO2
High CO2 + low pH → acute
High bicarbonate → chronic

cards.t:
Venous vs arterial gas
• What can a venous gas tell you?
• What can't it tell you?
cards.k:
Venous gas gives: pH, approximate CO2
Cannot assess: oxygenation (MJA 2015)

cards.t: Respiratory distress: which bedside tests in the first minutes?
cards.k:
12-lead ECG
Glucose
Bloods
Chest X-ray or bedside ultrasound

cards.t:
Respiratory distress: first move
• Wheeze
• Oedema
• Anaphylaxis
• Opioid excess
cards.k:
Wheeze → bronchodilator
Oedema → sit up + CPAP
Anaphylaxis → IM adrenaline
Opioid excess → support breathing + titrated naloxone per protocol

cards.t:
Oxygen ladder
• What is it?
• How do you climb it?
cards.k:
Cannula, Venturi or simple mask → non-rebreather → high-flow → CPAP or BiPAP → intubation
Move up one rung at a time

cards.t: Why use a Venturi mask for CO2 retainers?
cards.k:
Think of cordial mixed at the tap: fixed ratio → every glass the same strength
Venturi valve: jet of pure oxygen drags room air in through side holes → hole size sets the ratio (blue 24%, white 28%)
Flow is far more than the patient breathes in → breathing harder cannot change the mix
Result: fixed percentage → can hit 88 to 92% without overshooting
Simple mask or non-rebreather: varies or gives too much
Why it matters: too much oxygen in a CO2 retainer → CO2 rises → drowsy
(Standard teaching; flow per the valve or device label, not checked against a specific Australian product.)

cards.t:
CPAP vs BiPAP
• What does each pressure do?
• Which problem does each fix?
cards.k:
CPAP: one steady pressure keeps air spaces open → low oxygen from pulmonary oedema or pneumonia
BiPAP: adds a push on each breath in → high CO2 with a low pH
(Standard teaching.)

cards.t:
Oxygen devices
• Why do low-flow devices give a varying oxygen percentage?
• How is high-flow different?
• How does a Venturi mask fix it, and when do you use one?
cards.k:
Goal: control the oxygen % in each breath (room air is 21%), chosen to fit the patient
Low-flow (nasal cannula, simple mask): a breathless patient breathes in far faster than the set flow → room air fills the gap → the real % changes with every breath
(Your example: they pull about 30 to 40 L/min while the device gives a few. That figure is not verified against an Australian source.)
High-flow nasal oxygen: flow is higher than their demand → no room air drawn in → the set % is what they get
Venturi: lets in a fixed amount of room air on purpose → the % is fixed (settings 24 to 60%)
CO2 retainers (COPD and others at risk of hypercapnia): Venturi 24 to 28%, target SpO2 88 to 92%
Key: the danger is uncontrolled oxygen, not oxygen itself → the flow you set is not the flow they need
(Australian Prescriber, Acute use of oxygen therapy: Venturi 24–28% for COPD and others at risk of hypercapnic failure; SpO2 target 88–92%)

cards.t: Why must you not sedate a breathless, agitated patient?
cards.k:
Anxiety and agitation are often hypoxia or high CO2
→ do not sedate

cards.t: Sudden low saturation, clear chest, recent surgery: what do you think of first?
cards.k:
Sudden low saturation + clear chest + recent surgery
→ think pulmonary embolism before pneumonia

cards.t:
Respiratory distress: ICU outreach
• When do you call ICU outreach?
• What do you check early?
cards.k:
Call ICU outreach if: drowsy, silent chest, rising CO2 or falling pH, hypotension, oxygen need rising
Check treatment limits early
(Victoria: Adult Retrieval Victoria coordinates transfer of critically ill adults and gives phone advice, 1300 36 86 61. Confirm who calls at GV Health.)

cards.t: How do you hand over a breathless patient in 20 seconds?
cards.k:
Who → what you see → what you think → what you have done → what you need
Include the gas

cards.t:
Asthma severity
• How do you grade mild to moderate?
• How do you grade severe?
• How do you grade life-threatening?
cards.k:
Grade by the worst feature
Mild to moderate: full sentences, SpO2 over 94%
Severe: cannot finish a sentence, accessory muscles, SpO2 94% or below
Life-threatening: drowsy, exhausted, cyanosed, poor effort, or SpO2 under 92%

cards.t:
Asthma with a silent chest, drowsy or exhausted
• What does it mean?
• Who do you call?
cards.k:
Life-threatening: little air is moving
→ call ICU and your senior

cards.t: Asthma: which causes or complications do you look for?
cards.k:
Pneumothorax → suddenly worse or unequal air entry
Anaphylaxis
Pneumonia
Beta-blocker or NSAID

cards.t: Asthma: is a chest X-ray routine, and when do you do one?
cards.k:
Not routine
Only if you suspect pneumothorax or pneumonia

cards.t:
Mild to moderate asthma: salbutamol
• What dose?
• By what device?
• How often?
cards.k:
Salbutamol 4 to 12 puffs (100 micrograms each) by pMDI + spacer
Repeat every 20 minutes in the first hour if needed
Then every 4 to 6 hours

cards.t:
Severe asthma
• What salbutamol dose?
• What ipratropium dose?
• How often?
cards.k:
Salbutamol 12 puffs by spacer every 20 minutes in the first hour (or a 5 mg nebule if no spacer)
Plus ipratropium 8 puffs (21 micrograms each) every 20 minutes
Then 4 to 6 hourly

cards.t:
Life-threatening asthma
• What bronchodilators?
• How are they given?
• Where does the patient go?
cards.k:
Continuous nebulisation: 2 x 5 mg salbutamol nebules, oxygen-driven
Plus ipratropium 500 micrograms every 20 minutes for the first hour
Immediate transfer to higher-level care

cards.t:
Asthma and oxygen
• When do you start oxygen?
• What is the target?
cards.k:
Start if SpO2 under 92%
Target 92 to 96%
88 to 92% if CO2 retention is a risk

cards.t:
Asthma: oral steroid
• Which oral steroid?
• What dose?
• When?
• For how long?
cards.k:
Oral prednisolone early
Australian Prescriber: 50 mg first dose → then 25 mg twice daily, about 7 to 10 days
Confirm in your hospital protocol

cards.t:
Breathless asthmatic
• What does a normal CO2 mean?
• What does a rising CO2 mean?
cards.k:
They are tiring
Early in an attack: fast breathing blows off CO2 → CO2 should be low
Normal CO2 → can no longer keep that up
Rising CO2 → ventilation is failing

cards.t:
Asthma: IV magnesium
• When is it used?
• Who decides?
cards.k:
A senior decision
IV magnesium for severe attacks not responding
Dose per your hospital protocol (not verified here)

cards.t: Asthma: can you sedate a tiring patient?
cards.k:
Never
Benzodiazepines and opioids can precipitate respiratory arrest in a tiring asthmatic

cards.t:
Asthma suddenly worse with one side silent
• What do you think of?
• What do you do?
cards.k:
Think: tension pneumothorax
Signs: absent air entry one side, hypotension, neck veins
Decompress → do not send for an X-ray first

cards.t: Asthma discharge: what must be in place?
cards.k:
Never discharge on a reliever alone
Preventer with an inhaled steroid
Written action plan
Spacer technique
GP review within a few days

cards.t:
Acute asthma: reassessment
• When do you reassess?
• When do you escalate?
cards.k:
Reassess at 20 minutes, one hour, and after each change
Not improving at one hour → escalate

cards.t:
COPD flare
• What defines it?
• Which conditions mimic it?
• Which drug causes do you check for?
cards.k:
Flare: more breathless, more sputum, purulent sputum
Infection is common, but rule out mimics: heart failure, pneumonia, pneumothorax, PE, new arrhythmia such as AF (chest X-ray and ECG pick most up, NSW ACI)
Drug causes: missed inhalers, newly started beta-blocker, sedative (opioid or benzodiazepine) that slows breathing (drug list not in the NSW ACI page; check your hospital protocol)
Not responding → think of the mimics again

cards.t: COPD flare: what do you ask about early?
cards.k:
Treatment limits
Is ICU or intubation appropriate for this patient?

cards.t:
COPD flare: arterial gas
• When do you do one?
• What do you look at?
cards.k:
When: drowsy, severe, or low saturation
Look at: pH and CO2 before and after oxygen changes

cards.t: COPD flare: which tests?
cards.k:
Chest X-ray, ECG, bloods
Sputum culture if purulent
Troponin and BNP if unclear

cards.t:
COPD flare: oxygen
• What target?
• By which devices?
• Why avoid excess?
cards.k:
Target: 88 to 92%
Devices: nasal prongs 0.5 to 2 L/min, or Venturi 24% or 28%
Excess oxygen can worsen hypercapnia

cards.t:
COPD flare: bronchodilators
• What doses by spacer?
• What doses by nebuliser?
cards.k:
Salbutamol: spacer 400 to 800 micrograms, or nebulised 2.5 to 5 mg
Ipratropium: spacer 80 micrograms, or nebulised 500 micrograms
Titrate hourly to six-hourly

cards.t:
COPD flare: prednisolone
• What dose?
• For how long?
cards.k:
Prednisolone 40 to 50 mg daily
NSW ACI: up to two weeks is adequate; shorter courses are common
Follow your protocol

cards.t:
COPD flare: antibiotics
• When do you give one?
• Which one?
cards.k:
If the sputum is purulent
Cover typical and atypical organisms
Agent and dose per eTG and your hospital protocol

cards.t: COPD flare: when do you consider NIV?
cards.k:
Respiratory acidosis (NSW ACI: pH under 7.3 or worsening; many protocols start under 7.35 with a raised CO2)
Drowsiness
Severe breathlessness
Persistent hypoxaemia

cards.t:
COPD patient drowsy on high oxygen with a slow rate
• What is happening?
• What do you do?
cards.k:
Over-oxygenation
→ reduce to the target + check a gas

cards.t:
COPD on NIV
• What do you recheck, and when?
• What should happen?
• What if it does not?
cards.k:
Recheck: gas, breathing rate and effort, usually within an hour (timing per your unit's NIV protocol)
They should improve
Not improving or worse → call ICU → discuss intubation within the agreed treatment limits
(Victoria: Adult Retrieval Victoria coordinates transfer of critically ill adults and gives phone advice, 1300 36 86 61. Confirm who calls at GV Health.)

cards.t: COPD flare: what are the admission criteria?
cards.k:
Marked symptoms + failure at home
Loss of mobility, cannot eat or sleep
Altered mental state
Worsening hypoxaemia
Right heart failure or new arrhythmia

cards.t: COPD: what must happen before discharge?
cards.k:
Inhaler technique
Preventer plan
Smoking cessation
Vaccines
Pulmonary rehabilitation
Written action plan + early review

cards.t:
Pneumonia
• How does it present?
• What are its mimics?
cards.k:
Presents: fever, cough, focal signs, new shadow on X-ray
Mimics: heart failure, PE, aspiration, lung cancer, TB

cards.t: Pneumonia: which red flags mean hospital?
cards.k:
RR over 22, HR over 100
Confusion
SBP under 90, SpO2 under 92%
Multilobar X-ray
Vomiting, no social support, unstable comorbidities

cards.t:
Pneumonia: where to treat
• How does CURB-65 guide it?
• How does CORB guide it?
cards.k:
CURB-65: above 1 → inpatient; above 2 → consider HDU or ICU
CORB: confusion, SaO2 90% or below, RR 30 or more, low BP

cards.t: Pneumonia: which tests before antibiotics?
cards.k:
Chest X-ray, bloods
Blood cultures (if no delay)
Sputum culture
Admitted and sick → urine antigens + viral PCR

cards.t:
Mild CAP (TG v16)
• Which antibiotic?
• What dose?
• What alternatives?
• How long?
cards.k:
Amoxicillin 1 g orally 8-hourly
Atypical suspected or penicillin allergy → doxycycline 100 mg 12-hourly or clarithromycin 500 mg 12-hourly
Duration: 5 to 7 days (TG v16)

cards.t:
Moderate CAP
• Where is it treated?
• Which antibiotics?
• When do you step down?
cards.k:
Admit
IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 6-hourly + doxycycline
Improving → step down to oral amoxicillin
(2011 summary; check eTG)

cards.t:
Severe CAP
• Which antibiotics?
• Where is it treated?
• When do you call ID?
cards.k:
Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily + azithromycin 500 mg IV daily
HDU or ICU
ID if: allergic, returned traveller, Staph aureus risk
(2011 summary; check eTG)

cards.t: Pneumonia: when do you give oxygen?
cards.k: Give if SpO2 under 92% → to the target range

cards.t:
Pneumonia with sepsis
• What are the signs?
• What do you do?
cards.k:
Signs: shock, high lactate, organ dysfunction
→ sepsis pathway + antibiotics without delay

cards.t: Pneumonia not responding at 48 hours: what do you do?
cards.k:
Reassess
Repeat the X-ray and cultures
Mild CAP → add doxycycline or clarithromycin

cards.t:
Pneumonia not improving at 5 days
• What do you look for?
• With what?
cards.k:
Look for empyema or lung abscess
→ ultrasound or CT

cards.t: Pneumonia: when do you step down to oral antibiotics?
cards.k:
When clinically improving
Complete the course

cards.t:
After pneumonia
• When do you repeat the chest X-ray?
• For whom?
cards.k:
About 6 weeks, if the first film was abnormal
(TG via Medicine Today)

cards.t: Pneumonia: what do you offer before discharge?
cards.k:
Vaccines
Smoking cessation

cards.t:
Tension pneumothorax
• How do you diagnose it?
• Do you wait for imaging?
cards.k:
Clinical: shock, severe breathlessness, absent air entry one side, high airway pressures if ventilated
Do not wait for imaging

cards.t: What are the types of pneumothorax?
cards.k:
Primary: young, tall, thin
Secondary: lung disease
Traumatic
Iatrogenic
Tension

cards.t: How do you confirm a pneumothorax?
cards.k:
Upright chest X-ray
Bedside ultrasound → no lung sliding, lung point
CT if unclear and stable

cards.t:
Tension pneumothorax: decompression
• How do you decompress (needle, site)?
• What if no improvement?
cards.k:
Decompress → then drain
14 or 16 gauge cannula
Adult site per your protocol (Australian paediatric guideline: second intercostal space, mid-clavicular line, 90 degrees)
No improvement → second attempt about 1 cm away

cards.t: Small primary pneumothorax with little breathlessness: what do you do?
cards.k:
Observe
Discharge with early review if they can come back easily (NSW ACI)

cards.t:
Large or symptomatic primary pneumothorax, stable
• What do you do?
• How?
cards.k:
Aspirate with 14 to 16 gauge
Stop at: resistance, excessive cough, or 2.5 L
Repeat X-ray
Symptom-free → 2 to 6 hours observation

cards.t: Failed aspiration or a secondary pneumothorax: what do you do?
cards.k:
Small-bore drain + admit
All secondary pneumothoraces are admitted
Large or symptomatic → small-bore drain

cards.t:
Chest drain: site
• Where is the site?
• Where do you cut to avoid the nerve and vessels?
cards.k:
Site: fifth intercostal space, anterior to the mid-axillary line
Cut: incision above the lower rib → avoids the nerve and vessels
(PCH guideline)

cards.t:
Chest drain systems
• What does the single-chamber set-up add?
• What does the two-chamber set-up add?
• What does the three-chamber set-up add?
• What problem does each step fix?
cards.k:
Single chamber (underwater seal): air leaves, none returns; bubbles show air leaving
Problem → drained fluid raises the water level → air leaves with more difficulty
Two chambers: collection chamber before the seal → fluid drains and is measured separately
Problem → a large volume of compressible gas before the seal → less efficient at draining a pneumothorax
Three chambers: add a suction chamber with a regulator → fluid and air drain, suction is adjustable
(Source: Alfred ICU Academic Centre video: Chest Drains and Suction, Melbourne.)

cards.t:
Underwater seal drain
• How much water makes the seal?
• Where must it sit?
• What must you check after repositioning or transport?
cards.k:
Seal: about 2 to 3 cm of water → air leaves, none goes back in
Keep it below the patient's chest, otherwise fluid can be sucked back into the pleural space; keep it upright (a tipped bottle lets air back in)
May be clamped briefly to move the patient → always check it is unclamped afterwards
Trap: clamping a drain that still has an air leak (still bubbling) → the air cannot leave the pleura → it builds up → tension pneumothorax
(Source: Alfred ICU Academic Centre video: Chest Drains and Suction, Melbourne. Note: the RCH chest drain guideline says no clamps for transport because of this risk; follow your hospital protocol on clamping.)

cards.t:
Pneumothorax drain while walking or being transported
• What can replace the underwater seal bottle?
• Why?
cards.k:
Heimlich valve: a one-way valve → air leaves, none returns
Avoids the problem of the seal bottle tipping over and letting air back in
(Source: Alfred ICU Academic Centre video: Chest Drains and Suction, Melbourne.)

cards.t:
Chest drain suction
• In which patients is it used?
• At what pressure?
• When do you stop?
• Why is it not routine in awake patients?
cards.k:
Awake patients who can cough: rarely needed → a cough or strong breath out raises the chest pressure higher than ICU suction levels, which pushes air out through the drain
(Breathing in lowers chest pressure a little but the water seal stops air coming back.)
Sedated, ventilated patients: commonly -20 cm water until bubbling has stopped and the X-ray shows the pneumothorax resolved → then stop
Modern dry system: set at -20, adjustable -10 to -40; bellows moving confirms the suction is working
Risk of routine suction: re-expansion pulmonary oedema (NSW ACI)
(ICU practice from the video. Ward guidance says no routine suction. NSW ACI gives no pressure value, so follow your unit's suction order.)
(Source: Alfred ICU Academic Centre video: Chest Drains and Suction, Melbourne.)

cards.t:
Suction turned off
• What must you do with the suction tubing?
• Why?
cards.k:
Take the suction tubing off the drain system
Otherwise the system is closed → air cannot leave the pleural space
(NSW ACI: if suction is off, check the suction orders and resume as ordered.)
(Source: Alfred ICU Academic Centre video: Chest Drains and Suction, Melbourne.)

cards.t:
Bubbling in a chest drain
• What does it mean?
• When is it normal?
• How do you describe it?
cards.k:
Means: air leak from the pleural space, or a leak in the tube connections
Normal: at end-expiration in a spontaneously breathing patient, at peak inspiration if ventilated (NSW ACI)
Describe: intermittent or continuous, by how much air comes out
Some drains have an air leak scale of 1 to 5
(Source: Alfred ICU Academic Centre video: Chest Drains and Suction, Melbourne.)

cards.t:
Continuous bubbling in a chest drain
• How do you find the leak with a clamp?
• What does it mean if the bubbling stops?
• What does it mean if it carries on?
• Can you leave it clamped?
cards.k:
Check the connections and the insertion site first
Clamp briefly close to the skin, then at intervals down the tube (NSW ACI)
(Think of a vacuum hose: hand over the nozzle and the noise stops; a crack further along the hose and it keeps going.)
Stops when clamped near the skin → air is coming from the patient side (lung or insertion site) → tell your senior
Still bubbles → leak is in the tubing or a connection beyond the clamp → move the clamp further down
Never leave a bubbling drain clamped → risk of tension pneumothorax
(Many hospital protocols forbid clamping a bubbling drain at all. Check yours.)
(Source: Alfred ICU Academic Centre video: Chest Drains and Suction, Melbourne.)

cards.t:
Swinging in a chest drain
• What does it mean?
• Which way does it move when spontaneously breathing?
• Which way does it move when ventilated?
• Why does it matter?
cards.k:
Fluid moves with breathing in the tubing or the seal chamber
Spontaneously breathing: moves towards the patient on inspiration (negative pleural pressure)
Ventilated: moves away on inspiration (positive pressure)
Swinging → the drain is connected to the pleural pressure changes, so it is patent
(Source: Alfred ICU Academic Centre video: Chest Drains and Suction, Melbourne.)

cards.t:
Chest drain has stopped swinging
• What are the causes?
• What do you do if the patient is worse?
cards.k:
Causes: lung has re-expanded and blocks the holes, blocked or kinked tube, displaced drain (NSW ACI also lists suction being applied)
Check: kink, blockage, disconnection, tube depth and position
Patient worse → X-ray → call your senior
A blocked tube can lead to tension pneumothorax
(NSW ACI: disconnect from suction once a shift to confirm swing is present.)
(Source: Alfred ICU Academic Centre video: Chest Drains and Suction, Melbourne.)

cards.t:
Three-chamber drain: safety parts
• What does the positive pressure release valve do?
• What does the manual negative pressure vent do?
cards.k:
Positive pressure release valve → opens if pressure builds up, as in tension pneumothorax
Manual negative pressure vent → use when going from high suction to lower suction
(Source: Alfred ICU Academic Centre video: Chest Drains and Suction, Melbourne.)

cards.t: Ventilated patient with a sudden rise in airway pressure and low BP: what do you think of?
cards.k:
Sudden rise in airway pressure + hypotension
→ think tension pneumothorax

cards.t:
Removing a chest drain
• When do you remove it?
• What if the leak persists?
cards.k:
Lung up + no leak → remove
Persistent leak for days → involve cardiothoracic surgery

cards.t: Charting a chest drain: what do you record on every check?
cards.k:
Swinging: yes or no
Bubbling: none, intermittent or continuous (air leak 1 to 5 if the drain has a scale)
Fluid volume in the collection chamber
(Source: Alfred ICU Academic Centre video: Chest Drains and Suction, Melbourne.)

cards.t: After a pneumothorax: what advice do you give?
cards.k:
Stop smoking
Recurrence is common
Flying and diving → per your respiratory team

cards.t:
AKI: definition
• Which two measurements define it?
• What must you compare the creatinine with?
cards.k:
Rise in creatinine or fall in urine output → either counts
Compare with the patient's baseline creatinine, not the lab range
(KDIGO approach; the exact Australian wording was not checked.)

cards.t:
AKI staging by creatinine
• What multiple of baseline marks stage 1?
• What multiple marks stage 2?
• What multiple marks stage 3?
cards.k:
Stage 1: 1.5 to 1.9 times baseline (or rise of 26.5 micromol/L or more within 48 hours)
Stage 2: 2 to 2.9 times
Stage 3: 3 times or more, creatinine of 354 micromol/L or more, or starting dialysis
(Standard KDIGO teaching, not checked against the Australian text.)

cards.t: AKI staging by urine output: what output for how long marks each stage?
cards.k:
Stage 1: under 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 to 12 hours
Stage 2: under 0.5 mL/kg/h for 12 hours or more
Stage 3: under 0.3 mL/kg/h for 24 hours, or no urine for 12 hours
(Standard KDIGO teaching.)

cards.t:
AKI: causes
• What are the three groups of causes?
• What is one common ward example of each?
cards.k:
Pre-renal (low flow to kidney) → dehydration, sepsis, heart failure
Intrinsic (damage in kidney) → acute tubular necrosis, nephrotoxic drugs, glomerulonephritis
Post-renal (blocked outflow) → urinary retention, stones, blocked catheter

cards.t: AKI: which three drugs together classically cause pre-renal AKI in a dry patient?
cards.k:
ACE inhibitor or ARB + diuretic + NSAID
→ the 'triple whammy'

cards.t: AKI: which bedside checks do you do in the first hour?
cards.k:
Volume status: BP lying and standing, mucous membranes, JVP, oedema
Drug chart review
Bladder scan
Urine dipstick for blood and protein
Urine output chart

cards.t:
AKI: blood and protein on the dipstick
• What does it suggest?
• Who do you tell?
cards.k:
Blood and protein → intrinsic cause such as glomerulonephritis
→ tell your registrar and the renal team early

cards.t: AKI: when do you ask for a renal tract ultrasound?
cards.k:
When obstruction is possible or cause unclear → usually within 24 hours
Infected, obstructed kidney suspected → sooner

cards.t: Pre-renal AKI in a dry patient: how do you give fluid?
cards.k:
Measured boluses of 250 to 500 mL
Reassess after each: BP, urine output, signs of overload
Stop when euvolaemic

cards.t: AKI: which drugs do you withhold or adjust?
cards.k:
Withhold: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics (unless overloaded), NSAIDs, metformin
Avoid if you can: aminoglycosides, IV contrast
Adjust the dose of renally cleared drugs

cards.t:
AKI from urinary retention
• What do you do?
• What do you watch for afterwards?
cards.k:
Bladder scan → insert catheter, record volume drained
Then chart hourly urine output
Watch for large post-obstructive diuresis → dehydration, electrolyte loss

cards.t: AKI: which complications need an urgent call to your registrar or the renal team?
cards.k:
Potassium 6.5 or more, or ECG changes
Pulmonary oedema not responding
Severe acidosis
Uraemic signs (pericarditis, confusion)
Infected, obstructed kidney

cards.t: AKI: why is furosemide the wrong treatment for low urine output in a dry patient?
cards.k:
Diuretic does not treat the cause
Dry or hypotensive patient → lowers BP and kidney blood flow further

cards.t:
AKI recovery
• What do you do daily while it recovers?
• When do the withheld drugs restart?
cards.k:
Daily: creatinine, potassium, fluid balance, weight
Restart ACE inhibitors and diuretics only once creatinine has settled → often at a lower dose → repeat blood test afterwards
Write the drug hold and restart plan in the notes

cards.t:
Hyperkalaemia: severity
• What levels are mild?
• What levels are moderate?
• What levels are severe?
cards.k:
Mild: 5.5 to 5.9
Moderate: 6.0 to 6.4
Severe: 6.5 mmol/L and above
Any ECG change → emergency whatever the number
(NSW SESLHD.)

cards.t: Hyperkalaemia: what are the ECG changes, in the order they appear?
cards.k:
Tall peaked T waves
→ long PR, flat P waves
→ wide QRS
→ sine wave
→ VF or asystole

cards.t: Where is the body's potassium, and what moves it into cells?
cards.k:
About 98% is inside cells; plasma holds only a little (your note: about 12 mmol) → small shifts change the level a lot
Na-K ATPase pumps potassium in, sodium out
Insulin and beta-2 agonists switch it on → why insulin-dextrose and salbutamol lower potassium

cards.t:
Acidosis and potassium
• Which acidoses push potassium out of cells?
• Which barely do?
• Why the difference?
cards.k:
Mineral (normal anion gap) acidosis, such as diarrhoea or renal tubular acidosis → shifts potassium out
Why: H+ enters cells but chloride cannot follow → the cell becomes too positive → K+ leaves to balance the charge
Organic acids (lactate, ketones) → shift little potassium
Why: the acid enters with its own anion through a shared carrier (monocarboxylate transporter) → charge stays balanced → K+ stays in
High potassium in DKA → from lack of insulin and high glucose, not the ketoacidosis itself
Alkalosis → opposite, lowers potassium
(Standard teaching.)

cards.t:
High potassium result with a normal ECG and no risk factors
• What do you check before treating?
cards.k:
Was the sample haemolysed or delayed?
Repeat urgently (a blood gas gives a fast answer)
Do an ECG

cards.t: Hyperkalaemia: which drugs do you look for on the chart?
cards.k:
ACE inhibitors, ARBs
Spironolactone and other potassium-sparing diuretics
Trimethoprim
NSAIDs
Potassium supplements

cards.t:
How the kidney excretes potassium
• How does it excrete it?
• Which two things does it need?
• How does salt intake keep it steady?
cards.k:
Where: principal cells of the collecting duct
Sodium is pulled out of the urine → the tubule becomes negative → this pulls potassium into the urine
Aldosterone opens more sodium channels → speeds this up
So big potassium loss needs both: enough sodium reaching the duct and aldosterone
Normally they balance → high salt intake lowers aldosterone, low salt intake raises it → potassium loss stays steady
(Standard teaching.)

cards.t:
Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes
• What do you give first?
• What dose, and how fast?
• What does it not do?
cards.k:
Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL (2.2 mmol) IV over 2 to 3 minutes, on a monitor
Repeat ECG after 5 to 10 minutes → repeat the dose if still abnormal
Protects the heart, does not lower the potassium
(NSW SESLHD and Queensland Health.)

cards.t:
Hyperkalaemia: insulin and glucose
• What are the regimens in NSW?
• What are the regimens in Queensland?
cards.k:
NSW SESLHD: 10 units Actrapid in 50 mL of glucose 50% over 30 minutes
Queensland Health: 5 to 10 units with 50 mL of glucose 50% over 5 minutes → 5 units in kidney failure or under 50 kg
Use your own hospital protocol

cards.t:
After insulin and glucose for hyperkalaemia
• How do you monitor the glucose?
• Why?
cards.k:
Check before the dose
Then every 30 minutes for 2 hours (NSW) or at least hourly for 6 hours (Queensland)
Hypoglycaemia can come late, especially in kidney failure

cards.t:
Hyperkalaemia: salbutamol
• What is the dose?
• What is its role?
cards.k:
10 mg nebulised (Queensland Health)
Extra shifter added to insulin, not a replacement

cards.t:
Hyperkalaemia: sodium bicarbonate
• When is it used?
• How is it given?
cards.k:
