Only when there is a metabolic acidosis
50 mL of 8.4% IV over 5 to 15 minutes
Never a rapid large push
(NSW SESLHD.)

cards.t: Hyperkalaemia: which treatments actually remove potassium from the body?
cards.k:
Binding resin: Resonium A 15 g orally, up to three or four times a day in NSW
Dialysis
Stop the cause
Calcium and insulin only protect and shift

cards.t:
Hyperkalaemia: rechecking
• Why must you recheck after treatment?
• How often?
cards.k:
Insulin wears off in a few hours → potassium rebounds
Recheck every 2 hours (NSW), or hourly if severe (Queensland)
Until below 5.5

cards.t:
Hyperkalaemia: renal team and dialysis
• Who needs a call to the renal team or dialysis?
• What are the general urgent dialysis triggers (AEIOU)?
cards.k:
Hyperkalaemia → call renal for:
ECG changes
Potassium 6.5 or more that does not respond
Passes no urine
Any dialysis patient who has missed a session
AEIOU (general urgent dialysis triggers):
A → acidosis not responding to treatment
E → electrolytes: hyperkalaemia not responding
I → ingestions removed by dialysis (such as lithium, salicylate, toxic alcohols)
O → fluid overload not responding to diuretics
U → uraemic complications: pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding
(AEIOU is standard teaching; I did not find it in an Australian source. The cut-offs in your note (pH under 7.1, potassium 6.5) are commonly quoted: use your hospital protocol.)

cards.t:
ACE inhibitors, ARBs and spironolactone
• Why do they raise potassium in CKD?
• Why in heart failure?
cards.k:
CKD, heart failure, cirrhosis, volume depletion → less sodium reaches the collecting duct
The body compensates with high aldosterone → this keeps potassium excretion going
ACE inhibitor, ARB, spironolactone block aldosterone → that support is removed → potassium rises
Check potassium and creatinine after starting or increasing these drugs

cards.t: Hyperkalaemia from drugs in AKI: when do the drugs restart?
cards.k:
Restart only when potassium and creatinine are stable
Often at a lower dose
Check potassium a few days after restarting

cards.t:
Hypokalaemia: severity
• What levels are mild, moderate and severe?
• What makes any level urgent?
cards.k:
Mild: 3.0 to 3.4
Moderate: 2.5 to 2.9
Severe: below 2.5 mmol/L
ECG changes, symptoms or digoxin → urgent at any level
(Standard teaching.)

cards.t: Hypokalaemia: what are the ECG changes?
cards.k:
Flat T waves
→ ST depression, prominent U waves
→ ectopics, atrial or ventricular arrhythmias including torsades

cards.t:
Low potassium: causes
• What are the three groups of causes?
• Which other level do you check?
cards.k:
Low intake → rarely enough on its own; usually with vomiting or diuretics
Shift into cells
Losses → kidney, gut, skin
Check magnesium → low magnesium keeps potassium being lost in urine, hard to correct
(LITFL)

cards.t: Which causes shift potassium into cells?
cards.k:
Insulin (including refeeding syndrome)
Beta-2 agonists → salbutamol in asthma or COPD, beta-agonist tocolytics
Alkalosis
Fast new cell production → starting B12 or folate for megaloblastic anaemia
(LITFL for the first three; the B12 point is standard teaching, not on the Australian pages I checked.)

cards.t:
Low potassium in a patient on digoxin
• Why is it dangerous (the mechanism)?
• What do you do?
• Why not reach for amiodarone?
cards.k:
Why: K⁺ and digoxin compete for the same binding site on the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase
Low K⁺ → more digoxin binds → more pumps blocked → Na⁺ builds up inside the cell
→ the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger pushes out less Ca²⁺ → Ca²⁺ builds up → cells fire on their own → ectopics, VT, VF
(The stronger squeeze is the wanted effect; the arrhythmia comes from the calcium overload.)
Do: 12-lead ECG and a cardiac monitor (telemetry)
Hold the digoxin and the diuretic (furosemide)
Send a digoxin level, replace K⁺, check and replace Mg
Tell your registrar
No reflex amiodarone: it raises digoxin levels (the digoxin dose is usually halved when amiodarone starts)
(Sources: LITFL Pharm 101 digoxin; GPnotebook Australia, digoxin interactions.)

cards.t:
Vomiting and low potassium
• Why does it cause low potassium when gastric fluid holds little potassium?
• What are the three ways it happens?
cards.k:
Gastric fluid holds little potassium → the main loss is in the urine
Volume loss: kidney senses low volume → aldosterone rises → holds on to sodium and water, secretes potassium into the urine
Alkalosis: lost stomach acid → kidney excretes the extra bicarbonate → bicarbonate reaches the collecting duct with sodium → its negative charge in the tubule draws potassium out into the urine
Shift: alkalosis → cells release H+ and take up K+ → blood potassium falls further
(The shift is the smallest part; the urine loss is the main one.)
(Standard teaching; LITFL metabolic alkalosis.)

cards.t:
Hypokalaemia: replacement
• When is oral replacement enough?
• When do you go to IV?
cards.k:
Oral → mild or moderate, working gut, normal ECG
IV → severe, ECG changes, symptoms, or cannot take or absorb tablets
(Oral dose per your hospital protocol; not checked here.)

cards.t:
IV potassium on a general ward
• What concentration and rate?
• What are the two things you never do?
cards.k:
10 mmol in 100 mL over 1 hour through a peripheral line, premixed bag
Never a push
Never add it to a bag already running
(NSW potassium guidance.)

cards.t: IV potassium faster than 10 mmol an hour: what does it need?
cards.k:
Faster than 10 mmol an hour → monitored setting with continuous ECG
+ senior approval

cards.t:
Hypokalaemia that will not correct
• What do you check?
• What do you replace?
cards.k:
Check and replace magnesium
Low magnesium → kidney keeps losing potassium
(Dose per hospital protocol.)

cards.t: Replacing potassium in kidney failure: what is the risk?
cards.k:
Risk: overshooting into hyperkalaemia
→ replace in smaller amounts, recheck more often

cards.t:
Aldosterone and distal sodium
• When do they together cause a big potassium loss?
• How does primary aldosteronism fit?
cards.k:
Big potassium loss when both are high at once:
Diuretic (more sodium downstream) + high aldosterone (volume loss, heart failure, or primary aldosteronism)
Primary aldosteronism (Conn's adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia) → raises aldosterone by itself → retained sodium expands volume → body sends more sodium downstream → potassium keeps being lost
Look for high BP with low potassium
(LITFL lists these causes.)
One alone (only aldosterone, or only extra sodium) gives little potassium loss

cards.t:
Hypokalaemia: follow-up
• When do you recheck?
• What else must be fixed?
cards.k:
Recheck after each 20 to 40 mmol, and the next morning
Fix the cause: review diuretics, treat vomiting, diarrhoea or high-output stoma

cards.t:
Hyponatraemia: severity
• What levels are mild, moderate and severe?
• Which symptoms are an emergency?
cards.k:
Mild: 130 to 134
Moderate: 125 to 129
Severe: below 125 mmol/L
Seizure or coma → emergency whatever the number

cards.t: Hyponatraemia: which tests sort the type?
cards.k:
Serum osmolality → confirms a true low-sodium state
Urine osmolality + urine sodium
Cortisol + thyroid function → before calling it SIADH

cards.t: Hyponatraemia: what are the three volume groups, with a cause of each?
cards.k:
Dry (hypovolaemic) → vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics
Normal volume → SIADH, adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism
Wet (hypervolaemic) → heart failure, cirrhosis, kidney disease

cards.t: Hyponatraemia: which common drugs cause it?
cards.k:
Thiazides
SSRIs
Carbamazepine
Proton pump inhibitors

cards.t: SIADH: what do the urine osmolality and urine sodium show, and why is the urine sodium high, not low?
cards.k:
Euvolaemic patient
Urine osmolality: inappropriately concentrated, over 100 mmol/kg
Urine sodium: high, over 30 mmol/L
Normal cortisol and thyroid function, no diuretic
Why high: the kidney guards volume, not the sodium number
ADH holds extra water → body a little too full → kidney sheds sodium so water follows → urine sodium high
(NSW SESLHD POWH ED hyponatraemia summary and GPnotebook AU: urine osmolality over 100, urine sodium over 30, euvolaemic, normal adrenal and thyroid function.)

cards.t:
Hyponatraemia with a seizure or coma
• What do you give?
• How fast?
• How often can you repeat it?
cards.k:
Hypertonic saline 3%: 150 mL IV over 20 minutes
Check sodium after each bolus
Repeat up to twice
(NSW SESLHD.)

cards.t:
Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia
• What rise are you aiming for in the first hour?
• Then what?
cards.k:
Aim: about 5 mmol/L rise in the first hour → then stop the hypertonic saline
Goal is to stop the seizure, not reach a normal sodium
(NSW SESLHD.)

cards.t:
SIADH
• What is the treatment?
• Why is 0.9% saline the wrong fluid?
cards.k:
Fluid restriction + treat the cause
0.9% saline is wrong: kidney passes the salt, keeps the water → sodium can fall further
(Restriction volume per hospital protocol; not checked here.)

cards.t:
Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia
• What fluid do you give?
• Why can the sodium then rise too fast?
• What do you watch for?
cards.k:
Fluid: 0.9% saline → refills the circulation
Before: low volume → high ADH → kidney holds water even though it dilutes the sodium (blood pressure wins over sodium)
Volume back → ADH switches off
→ kidney dumps dilute urine (aquaresis), the salt stays → sodium rises fast → risk of osmotic demyelination
Watch: urine output → a sudden surge of pale, dilute urine is the early warning (your note says over 100 to 150 mL/h; that cut-off is not verified here, use your hospital protocol)
Sodium: every 2 to 4 hours; limits as in the max-rise card (no more than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours, lower in high-risk patients)
(SESLHD RHW CLIN134 2025: rapid correction can switch off ADH → sudden massive diuresis → overly rapid sodium rise; check sodium and water balance 2 to 4 hourly.)

cards.t:
Any hyponatraemia
• Which IV fluids do you stop?
• Why do they lower the sodium further?
cards.k:
Stop hypotonic fluids: glucose 5%, 0.45% saline, glucose-saline (4% glucose in 0.18% saline)
Glucose 5%: the glucose is taken up by cells → what stays behind is plain water
0.45% saline: half the salt of plasma → more water than salt
Both act as free water → blood more dilute → sodium falls → brain swelling risk
(Exception: a senior may give hypotonic fluid on purpose to bring an overcorrected sodium back down.)
(MJA, Hilton et al: avoid all hypotonic fluids while the sodium is low or falling.)

cards.t:
Sodium correction limit
• What is the maximum rise in 24 hours?
• In whom is it lower?
• Why are they at higher risk?
cards.k:
No more than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours
8 in high-risk patients: alcohol dependence, malnutrition, liver disease, low potassium (also sodium 105 or below)
(SESLHD aims even lower in high-risk patients: 4 to 6 mmol/L a day.)
Why: in chronic low sodium, brain cells shed osmolytes to stop swelling
Correction → water leaves brain cells → they must rebuild those osmolytes
Too fast → cells shrink → myelin stripped (osmotic demyelination, often in the pons)
High-risk groups rebuild osmolytes poorly: little energy or nutrients, sick astrocytes in liver disease
Low potassium: replacing potassium also pushes the sodium up → count it in the plan
(The reasons each group is at risk come from your note and standard physiology; not verified against an Australian source.)
(NSW SESLHD.)

cards.t:
Correcting a low sodium too fast
• What is the danger?
• When does it show?
cards.k:
Osmotic demyelination
Weakness, speech and swallowing problems, locked-in state → appears days later
Cannot be reversed

cards.t:
During sodium correction
• How often do you check the sodium?
• Which bedside sign warns of overcorrection?
• Why does it happen?
cards.k:
Every 2 to 4 hours (and after each bolus in a severe case)
Warning sign: sudden large output of dilute urine → sodium about to rise fast
Why: the trigger for ADH is fixed (volume restored, pain or nausea treated, thiazide stopped) → ADH switches off
→ kidney passes free water (aquaresis) and keeps the salt → sodium climbs even with the drip off
Blood results lag → act on the urine bag: recheck the sodium now and tell your registrar
(Society for Endocrinology 2022: rising urine output is an early sign of aquaresis. A threshold such as over 100 mL an hour is often quoted but was not found in an Australian source; use your hospital protocol.)

cards.t: The sodium is rising too fast: what do you do?
cards.k:
Stop the hypertonic saline
Check sodium hourly
Call your registrar
Desmopressin and glucose 5% can bring it back → senior decision
(Regimen not checked here.)

cards.t: Reading a blood gas: what four questions do you ask, in order?
cards.k:
1 → Is the pH low or high?
2 → Did the CO2 or the bicarbonate move it?
3 → Is the other side compensating as much as expected?
4 → If metabolic acidosis → what is the anion gap?

cards.t:
Low pCO2 in a metabolic acidosis
• What does it mean?
• Name two causes
cards.k:
pCO2 lower than expected → second problem: respiratory alkalosis
Causes: salicylate poisoning, sepsis, pain or anxiety

cards.t: The pCO2 is higher than expected in a metabolic acidosis: what does that mean?
cards.k:
pCO2 higher than expected → added respiratory acidosis
Patient is tiring or breathing is depressed
Warning sign

cards.t:
Anion gap
• How do you calculate it?
• What is normal?
cards.k:
Anion gap = sodium − chloride − bicarbonate
Normal about 8 to 12 (check your lab)
Low albumin → lowers the normal value

cards.t:
Acid-base basics
• What sets the pH?
• Which buffers carry the acid load?
cards.k:
pH depends on the ratio of bicarbonate to CO2 (Henderson-Hasselbalch)
→ rises with bicarbonate; falls as CO2 (and H+) rises
Bicarbonate is the buffer you measure; haemoglobin, phosphate and proteins also buffer, and much buffering happens inside cells
Lungs → clear CO2
Kidney → keeps or excretes bicarbonate over hours to days

cards.t: Do extra haemoglobin or phosphate change the pH, since they are buffers too?
cards.k:
Not in a way that matters
All the buffers share the same hydrogen ions → they move together
So the bicarbonate and CO2 you measure already tell you the pH (isohydric principle)
Bicarbonate is the one that matters clinically because the lungs and the kidneys can change it
(Standard physiology teaching; not an Australian source.)

cards.t:
Checking a gas
• How do you check pH, pCO2 and bicarbonate agree, using the hydrogen ion formula?
cards.k:
Hydrogen ion (nmol/L) = 24 x pCO2 / bicarbonate
Normal: 24 x 40 / 24 = 40 nmol/L → pH 7.40
Hydrogen ion about 50 → pH about 7.30
Hydrogen ion about 32 → pH about 7.50
The three numbers should fit → if not, query the sample
(Standard formula; not an Australian source.)

cards.t:
Respiratory acidosis
• How much should bicarbonate rise per 10 mmHg CO2, acute?
• How much, chronic?
• Why the difference?
cards.k:
Bicarbonate rise per 10 mmHg CO2 rise:
Acute → 1 mmol/L (range 1 to 2)
Chronic (after a few days) → 3 to 4 (Brandis uses 4)
Why: kidney needs days to hold bicarbonate → an acute CO2 rise drops the pH far more than the same rise in chronic COPD
(Brandis, Acid-base Physiology, and the Merck Manual (3 to 4); corrected from your note, which had 2 for chronic.)

cards.t:
Respiratory alkalosis
• How much should bicarbonate fall per 10 mmHg CO2, acute?
• How much, chronic?
cards.k:
Bicarbonate falls per 10 mmHg fall in CO2:
Acute → about 2 mmol/L (range 1 to 2)
Chronic (2 to 3 days) → 4 to 5
Acute respiratory alkalosis: bicarbonate rarely below about 18 → lower means a metabolic acidosis as well
(Brandis and the Merck Manual (4 to 5); corrected from your note, which had 3 and 4.)

cards.t:
Two patients, both with a pCO2 of 80
• How do the bicarbonate and pH show which is acute?
• Which is chronic?
cards.k:
Acute → bicarbonate about 28 → pH about 7.16
Chronic → bicarbonate about 38 → pH about 7.30
Bicarbonate shows how long the kidney has had to compensate
In between → acute on chronic (a COPD patient who is getting worse)
(Calculated from hydrogen ion = 24 x pCO2 / bicarbonate, using acute +1 and chronic +3.5 per 10 mmHg; see the Acid-base lab.)

cards.t:
Compensation by breathing
• What CO2 do you expect in metabolic acidosis?
• What CO2 do you expect in metabolic alkalosis?
cards.k:
Acidosis (Winter's): expected pCO2 = 1.5 x bicarbonate + 8 (plus or minus 2)
Alkalosis: expected pCO2 = 0.7 x bicarbonate + 20 (plus or minus 5)
CO2 outside the range → a second, respiratory problem
(Brandis)

cards.t:
COPD patient on high-flow oxygen, drowsy, pH 7.24, pCO2 78, bicarbonate 34
• What is this?
• What do you do first?
cards.k:
Acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis, worsened by too much oxygen
Titrate oxygen to 88 to 92% (do not remove it)
Call your senior
Repeat the gas in 30 to 60 minutes
NIV if pH stays below 7.35

cards.t:
Compensation
• Why is it 'never complete'?
• What do clinicians mean by 'compensated'?
cards.k:
Compensation moves pH towards normal, not all the way → pH still points to the primary problem
On the ward, 'compensated' loosely = pH in range, CO2 and bicarbonate abnormal
Fully normal pH + clearly abnormal CO2 and bicarbonate → look for two disorders

cards.t:
High anion gap acidosis with a near-normal bicarbonate or a normal pH
• How do you find a hidden metabolic alkalosis?
cards.k:
High-gap acidosis + metabolic alkalosis (e.g. vomiting) can cancel out → normal pH
Delta ratio = rise in AG / fall in HCO3
1 to 2 → pure high anion gap acidosis
Above 2 → bicarbonate started high → metabolic alkalosis too (e.g. DKA with vomiting)
0.4 to 0.8 → high and normal gap acidosis together
Below 0.4 → normal gap acidosis
'Corrected bicarbonate' (measured HCO3 + extra anion gap): well above normal → alkalosis
(LITFL)

cards.t: After acting on a blood gas: when do you repeat it?
cards.k: Usually 30 to 60 minutes after the change in treatment

cards.t: Metabolic acidosis: what are the two ways it happens, with examples of each?
cards.k:
Acid added (high anion gap): lactate, ketones, renal failure, toxins
Bicarbonate lost (normal anion gap):
Gut → diarrhoea, fistulas, drains, ileostomy (lower gut fluid is bicarbonate-rich)
Kidney → renal tubular acidosis, acetazolamide
(Vomiting loses acid → alkalosis, not acidosis)

cards.t:
Hydrogen ion in a metabolic acidosis
• Why does it lower the bicarbonate?
• Why does it raise the anion gap?
• Why does it always come with an anion?
cards.k:
Acids (lactic, keto) come as a hydrogen ion plus an anion → free hydrogen ions do not exist alone
Hydrogen takes a bicarbonate → CO2 and water → bicarbonate falls
The anion (lactate, ketone) stays behind → not measured → anion gap rises
The fall in bicarbonate is roughly equal to the rise in the gap
(Standard teaching; not an Australian source.)

cards.t:
Diarrhoea vs vomiting
• Why does diarrhoea cause an acidosis?
• Why does vomiting cause an alkalosis?
• What happens to the chloride?
cards.k:
Stomach → makes acid; everything after it (pancreas, bile, small bowel, colon) makes bicarbonate-rich fluid
Vomiting → loses stomach acid → alkalosis
Diarrhoea, fistulas, ileostomy, drains → lose bicarbonate → acidosis
Bicarbonate lost, no new anion → kidney keeps chloride → chloride rises → normal gap (hyperchloraemic)
(Standard teaching; not an Australian source.)

cards.t:
Acetazolamide
• How does it cause a normal-gap acidosis?
• Why does the potassium fall with it?
cards.k:
Blocks carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule → filtered bicarbonate is not reclaimed → lost in the urine
Kidney keeps chloride in its place → normal-gap (hyperchloraemic) acidosis, like a proximal (type 2) RTA
Potassium falls → more sodium and bicarbonate reach the collecting duct, and the volume loss raises aldosterone → sodium is taken back in exchange for potassium → potassium lost in urine
The distal tubule cannot make enough new bicarbonate to make up for the proximal loss
Self-limiting: as blood bicarbonate falls, less is filtered, so the loss slows
Same effect used on purpose: a senior may add it for alkalosis in heart failure on high-dose diuretics (check potassium first)
(From your pasted Gemini note, rewritten. Standard renal physiology; not checked against an Australian source. Left out: the note's claim that distal acid is 'flushed out' in the urine.)

cards.t: Why does low aldosterone cause a normal-gap acidosis with a high potassium?
cards.k:
Aldosterone makes the kidney keep sodium and pass out potassium and hydrogen ions
Too little (Addison disease, spironolactone, ACE inhibitors) → both potassium and acid held back
Result → high potassium + normal-gap acidosis
(Standard teaching; not an Australian source.)

cards.t:
Anion gap
• How do you calculate it?
• Why does it rise when acid is added?
• Why not when bicarbonate is lost?
cards.k:
AG = Na − (Cl + HCO3)
About 4 to 12 mmol/L without potassium with modern analysers (check whether your lab includes K and its range)
Acid added → H+ uses up bicarbonate, its anion (lactate, ketone) is unmeasured → gap rises
Bicarbonate lost → chloride rises in its place → gap stays normal (hyperchloraemic)
(LITFL)

cards.t:
Anion gap formula
• Why does it use only sodium, chloride and bicarbonate?
• What changes if your lab includes potassium?
cards.k:
Sodium is the main cation → potassium, calcium and magnesium are small and steady, so most formulas leave them out
Gap = unmeasured anions (mostly albumin, plus lactate, ketones and others)
If the lab adds potassium → its normal range is higher by about 4 → use the range printed on the report
A Western Australian guide gives 8 plus or minus 4 (4 to 12) without potassium
(Australian labs have no agreed common range; not checked against RCPA.)

cards.t:
Low albumin
• Why does it lower the anion gap?
• How do you correct the gap?
• Why does it matter in liver disease?
cards.k:
Why: albumin is the main unmeasured anion → plasma is always electrically neutral, and albumin carries many negative charges
Normal albumin (about 40 g/L) makes up most of the normal gap → each 10 g/L fall lowers the gap by about 2.5
Corrected AG = AG + 0.25 x (40 − albumin in g/L) (LITFL)
Why it matters: cirrhosis, sepsis, malnutrition → albumin often 20 or less
Example: albumin 20 → baseline gap about 8; a GI bleed adds lactate, +10 → gap reads 18 → looks only mildly high → corrected 18 + 5 = 23
Without correcting, lactate from a GI bleed or sepsis, or uraemia from hepatorenal syndrome, gets missed
(Corrected from your note: 'x 3' works with albumin in g/dL; Australian labs report g/L. US texts write the same rule as AG + 2.5 x (4.0 − albumin in g/dL).)

cards.t:
High-gap acidosis
• How do you work out where the bicarbonate should be?
• What does it tell you if it comes out higher?
• What does it tell you if it comes out lower?
cards.k:
Each unit of acid that raised the gap used up about one unit of bicarbonate
Should be = 24 minus the extra gap (gap minus about 12)
Comes out higher than that → something else was adding bicarbonate: a metabolic alkalosis (for example vomiting)
Comes out lower → bicarbonate was lost another way: a normal-gap acidosis as well
We are not correcting the bicarbonate → we use it as a clue
Example: DKA with vomiting → Na 138, Cl 88, HCO3 24 → gap 26 → extra 14 → should be 10 → comes out 24, 14 higher
(Same sum added back: 24 + 14 = 38; above about 29 counts as high. Delta gap method, Merck Manual; not an Australian source.)

cards.t:
High anion gap acidosis
• Which causes do you check for?
• With which test?
cards.k:
Lactate (sepsis, shock) → lactate level
Ketones (DKA, alcohol, starvation) → blood ketones, glucose
Renal failure → urea, creatinine
Toxins:
Methanol, ethylene glycol → osmolar gap; call Poisons Information 13 11 26
Salicylate → level
Paracetamol, metformin, iron
LITFL uses CAT MUDPILES; your PLUMSEEDS covers the same ground

cards.t:
Normal anion gap acidosis
• What are the causes (HARDASS)?
• Why does the gap stay normal (show it with the gap formula and acetazolamide)?
• How do you tell gut from kidney?
cards.k:
HARDASS:
H → hyperalimentation (parenteral nutrition, amino acid infusions)
A → Addison's or hypoaldosteronism
R → renal tubular acidosis (types 1, 2 and 4)
D → diarrhoea, fistulas, ileostomy, drains
A → acetazolamide
S → spironolactone (and other potassium-sparing diuretics)
S → saline in large volumes (chloride load)
Why the gap stays normal: bicarbonate is lost, or acid is not excreted, with no new anion → blood must stay neutral → kidney keeps chloride instead → hyperchloraemic
Gap = Na − (Cl + HCO3) → HCO3 falls, Cl rises by about the same → gap unchanged
Example (acetazolamide): kidney normally takes back filtered bicarbonate in the proximal tubule → acetazolamide blocks that → bicarbonate leaks into the urine → blood bicarbonate falls
Gut vs kidney: urine anion gap (Na + K − Cl) → low = gut, raised = kidney
(LITFL; corrected from your note: hypoaldosteronism and RTA give a normal anion gap, not a high one. DKA gives a high one. Your later note listed RTA types 1 and 4 only; proximal type 2, for example from acetazolamide, also counts.)

cards.t: Lactic acidosis from sepsis: what is the treatment?
cards.k:
Treat the sepsis: cultures → antibiotics within the hour → measured fluid boluses → repeat lactate
Not bicarbonate

cards.t:
Alcoholic ketoacidosis
• What do you give?
• In what order?
cards.k:
Thiamine first → then fluids with glucose → replace potassium and magnesium
No insulin: glucose is normal or low
(Thiamine dose per hospital protocol.)

cards.t:
Normal-gap acidosis from diarrhoea
• What fluid?
• What else do you replace?
cards.k:
Balanced fluid such as Hartmann's → rather than large volumes of 0.9% saline (adds chloride)
Replace potassium

cards.t: Acidosis with a kidney injury in a patient on metformin: what do you do with the metformin?
cards.k: Stop it

cards.t:
Bicarbonate in metabolic acidosis
• Why is it rarely first-line?
• How is it given if a senior wants it?
cards.k:
Why rarely first-line: does not fix lactate or ketones, can lower potassium, raises CO2
If a senior wants it: 50 mL of 8.4% slowly over 5 to 15 minutes → never a 100 mL push
Mainly considered in severe acidosis with kidney injury or high potassium
(No Australian threshold was verified.)

cards.t: An unexplained high-gap acidosis or suspected toxic alcohol: who do you call?
cards.k:
Your senior
Poisons Information Centre 13 11 26

cards.t: Metabolic acidosis: which findings mean you call your registrar now?
cards.k:
pH under 7.2
Lactate above 4
Shock not responding to the first boluses
Patient tiring (rising pCO2)
(Victoria: Adult Retrieval Victoria coordinates transfer of critically ill adults and gives phone advice, 1300 36 86 61. Confirm who calls at GV Health.)

cards.t: Severe metabolic alkalosis: what symptoms and signs can it cause?
cards.k:
Tetany and cramps (ionised calcium falls)
Weakness
Arrhythmias
Slow breathing

cards.t: Metabolic alkalosis: what are the ways it happens, with examples?
cards.k:
Acid lost: vomiting or NG aspirate; urine (diuretics, mineralocorticoid excess)
H+ shifted into cells: low potassium
Bicarbonate gained: given directly, or made by the liver from lactate or citrate (large volumes of Hartmann's, massive transfusion)
Fast correction of chronic CO2 retention
(Standard teaching.)

cards.t:
Metabolic alkalosis from ward treatments
• Which treatments can cause it?
• How?
cards.k:
Hartmann or Ringer lactate in large volumes → liver turns lactate into bicarbonate
Massive blood transfusion → citrate turned into bicarbonate
Parenteral nutrition → acetate turned into bicarbonate
Bicarbonate given directly
(Standard teaching; not an Australian source.)

cards.t:
Metabolic alkalosis on a gas
• How much should the pCO2 rise to compensate?
• What is the upper limit?
• Which electrolytes usually come with it?
cards.k:
High pH, high bicarbonate
pCO2 rises about 0.7 for each 1 mmol/L rise in bicarbonate
Rarely above about 55 mmHg from compensation alone → higher means a respiratory acidosis as well
Usually comes with low potassium and low chloride
(Study Kit; standard teaching, not checked against an Australian source.)

cards.t:
Urine chloride under 20 mmol/L
• What does it mean?
• What are the causes?
cards.k:
Urine chloride under 20 → chloride-responsive (volume depleted)
Causes: vomiting, nasogastric losses, past diuretic use
(Usual cut-off; standard teaching.)

cards.t:
Urine chloride over 20 mmol/L
• What does it mean?
• What are the causes?
cards.k:
Urine chloride over 20 → chloride-resistant
Causes: hyperaldosteronism, Cushing syndrome, severe potassium loss
Or a diuretic taken in the last day or two → result misleading

cards.t:
Loop or thiazide diuretic alkalosis
• How does it start?
• What keeps it going?
• Why does the urine chloride mislead you while the diuretic is acting?
cards.k:
Starts: diuretic → kidney loses sodium, chloride and water → volume and chloride fall
Low volume → aldosterone rises, and more sodium reaches the collecting duct → swapped for potassium and hydrogen ions → acid and potassium lost in urine → bicarbonate left behind
Keeps going: low volume, low chloride and low potassium all stop the kidney getting rid of the extra bicarbonate
Trap: while the diuretic is acting, urine chloride is high even though the patient is volume depleted → looks chloride-resistant
Once the diuretic wears off (a day or two) → urine chloride falls under 20 → chloride-responsive
(Study Kit; standard teaching, not checked against an Australian source.)

cards.t:
Metabolic alkalosis kept going by vomiting and diuretics
• Why do they keep it going?
• What fixes it?
cards.k:
Lose volume and chloride → kidney holds sodium under aldosterone
Sodium reaching the collecting duct + high aldosterone → drives potassium and H+ into urine
Low chloride → kidney cannot get rid of the extra bicarbonate
Low potassium → H+ moves into cells → worsens it
Fix: saline + potassium
(Corrected from your note: diuretics do not shift sodium into cells; they lose sodium, chloride, potassium and H+ in the urine.)

cards.t: Why must potassium be replaced before a metabolic alkalosis will correct?
cards.k:
Low potassium → hydrogen ions move into cells to take its place → blood becomes more alkaline
Kidney secretes hydrogen ions instead of potassium → makes new bicarbonate
Saline alone will not correct it while potassium is low
(Standard teaching; not an Australian source.)

cards.t: Chloride-responsive alkalosis: what is the treatment?
cards.k:
0.9% saline → chloride and volume
Potassium and magnesium replacement
Replace ongoing nasogastric losses while the cause is treated

cards.t: Chloride-resistant alkalosis with hypertension and low potassium: what do you do?
cards.k:
Replace potassium
Check magnesium
Investigate excess aldosterone (aldosterone and renin, cortisol) with endocrinology
Saline does not help and can raise the BP

cards.t: Alkalosis in an overloaded heart failure patient on high-dose diuretics: what are the options?
cards.k:
Reduce the diuretic if the oedema allows
Replace potassium
Senior may add acetazolamide
Do not give saline

cards.t: Metabolic alkalosis: which fluids and drugs do you avoid?
cards.k:
Bicarbonate
More loop diuretic
Hypotonic fluids such as glucose 5%

cards.t:
Excess mineralocorticoid (Conn's, steroids, liquorice)
• How does it cause alkalosis?
• How does it cause low potassium?
cards.k:
Aldosterone → collecting duct reabsorbs sodium, secretes potassium (principal cells) and H+ (intercalated cells)
Too much → both lost in urine → low potassium + metabolic alkalosis, usually high BP
Saline does not correct it (chloride-resistant)
(Standard teaching.)

cards.t:
Post-hypercapnic alkalosis
• What is it?
• Why only after chronic CO2 retention?
cards.k:
Chronic CO2 retention → kidney builds up high bicarbonate
CO2 brought down quickly (NIV or ventilator) → bicarbonate stays high for days → alkalosis
Acute retention → bicarbonate never rose much → does not happen
(Answers your question about chronic only.)

cards.t:
Metabolic alkalosis hiding behind an acidosis
• In which setting does it happen?
• How do you find it?
cards.k:
Example: diabetic ketoacidosis with vomiting → ketoacids pull the bicarbonate down → it can look normal
Work out where the bicarbonate should be → 24 minus the extra anion gap → if it comes out higher, the alkalosis was there too
Na 138, Cl 88, HCO3 24 → gap 26 → extra 14 → should be 10 → comes out 24
(Same sum added back: 24 + 14 = 38; above about 29 counts as high. Delta gap method, Merck Manual; not an Australian source.)

cards.t: Why can feeding after a period of starvation cause a mild alkalosis?
cards.k:
Fasting → ketoacids build up, body keeps their anions
Carbohydrate given → anions metabolised → regenerates bicarbonate → pH can overshoot into mild alkalosis
(Standard teaching; I could not check it against an Australian source.)

cards.t: Metabolic alkalosis: when do you call your registrar?
cards.k:
pH over 7.55
ECG changes or tetany
Hypertension + low potassium + high urine chloride

cards.t: Hypernatraemia: what are the three groups of causes?
cards.k:
Water loss with poor intake → dehydration, fever, cannot reach a drink
Water loss through the kidney → high glucose, diabetes insipidus
Salt gain → hypertonic saline or bicarbonate (rare)

cards.t: Hypernatraemia: what levels are mild, moderate and severe?
cards.k:
Mild: 146 to 150
Moderate: 151 to 159
Severe: 160 mmol/L and above
(Standard teaching.)

cards.t: Hypernatraemia: what do you assess at the bedside first?
cards.k:
Shocked? BP, pulse
Conscious level
Urine volume and concentration

cards.t: What findings suggest diabetes insipidus?
cards.k:
High sodium + very large output of dilute urine
Over 3 L a day or about 200 mL an hour
Urine osmolality below 300 mmol/kg

cards.t:
Diabetes insipidus
• What are the causes of the central type?
• What are the causes of the nephrogenic type?
cards.k:
Central → head injury, pituitary surgery
Nephrogenic → lithium, hypercalcaemia

cards.t: Hypernatraemia with shock: what fluid comes first?
cards.k:
0.9% saline in boluses until perfusion is restored
Free water comes after

cards.t: Hypernatraemia, not shocked: how do you replace the water?
cards.k:
Oral or enteral water if the patient can take it
Otherwise glucose 5% IV, at a rate agreed with your senior

cards.t:
Central diabetes insipidus
• What is the treatment?
• Who decides?
cards.k:
Water replacement + hourly urine output + frequent sodium checks
Desmopressin treats the cause → dose decided with your registrar and the endocrine or surgical team
Never restrict fluids

cards.t:
Chronic hypernatraemia
• How fast can the sodium fall?
• What is the danger of going faster?
cards.k:
No more than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours (about 0.5 an hour)
Faster fall → water moves into brain cells → cerebral oedema, seizures
(Standard teaching; not checked against an Australian source.)

cards.t: Treating hypernatraemia: how often do you check the sodium?
cards.k:
Every 4 to 6 hours
More often if it is falling fast

cards.t: Hypernatraemia: what do you fix besides the sodium?
cards.k:
Fix the cause: infection, high glucose, drugs
And the reason the patient could not drink

cards.t:
Hypercalcaemia: values
• Which calcium value do you use?
• What levels are mild, moderate and severe?
cards.k:
Use the corrected (albumin-adjusted) calcium
Mild: 2.6 to 2.9
Moderate: 3.0 to 3.4
Severe: 3.5 mmol/L and above
(UK Society for Endocrinology; no Australian source checked.)

cards.t:
Hypercalcaemia
• What are the symptoms?
• What is the ECG change?
cards.k:
Symptoms: thirst, polyuria, constipation, nausea, abdominal pain, confusion
ECG: short QT

cards.t:
Hypercalcaemia: causes
• What are the two commonest causes?
• Which drugs contribute?
cards.k:
Cancer → commonest in hospital
Primary hyperparathyroidism → commonest in the community
Drugs: thiazides, calcium and vitamin D supplements, lithium

cards.t: Hypercalcaemia: what does the PTH tell you?
cards.k:
High or normal PTH → primary hyperparathyroidism
Low (suppressed) PTH → cancer or vitamin D excess

cards.t: Hypercalcaemia: which other tests look for the cause?
cards.k:
Calcium, albumin, phosphate, kidney function
Serum protein electrophoresis + free light chains (myeloma)
Chest X-ray

cards.t:
Moderate or severe hypercalcaemia
• What is the first treatment?
• How much?
cards.k:
0.9% saline IV, about 4 to 6 L over 24 hours
Check for overload after each litre
Less in heart or kidney failure
(UK Society for Endocrinology.)

cards.t: Hypercalcaemia: which drugs do you stop?
cards.k:
Thiazides
Calcium
Vitamin D

cards.t:
Hypercalcaemia after fluids
• What drug lowers the calcium?
• At what dose and rate?
• How long does it take to work?
cards.k:
Zoledronic acid 4 mg IV over at least 15 minutes
After rehydration; dose adjusted for kidney function
Works in 2 to 4 days
(UK Society for Endocrinology.)

cards.t: Hypercalcaemia: when are steroids used?
cards.k:
Lymphoma, myeloma, sarcoid, vitamin D excess → steroids
Primary hyperparathyroidism → not for steroids

cards.t: Hypercalcaemia: why is furosemide not used first?
cards.k:
Patient is dry → loop diuretic worsens dehydration and kidney injury
Use only for fluid overload

cards.t: Mild hypercalcaemia with a raised PTH: what is the plan?
cards.k:
Stop contributing drugs
Oral fluids
Repeat calcium
Refer to endocrinology or surgery for primary hyperparathyroidism
No bisphosphonate or large-volume saline

cards.t:
DKA and potassium
• Why can it be high, normal or low?
• When must you not start insulin?
cards.k:
Total body potassium is low (lost in urine)
Insulin lack + high glucose hold potassium outside cells → blood level can look normal or high
Insulin drives it back in → level falls fast
NSW ACI: no insulin infusion until K is above 3.5 mmol/L
Replace potassium by level; check every 1 to 2 hours on a monitor
(Corrected from your note: ketoacids shift little potassium; the high level comes mainly from insulin lack and high glucose.)

cards.t: Renal colic: what is the typical picture?
cards.k:
Sudden loin pain → spreads to the groin, in waves
Cannot lie still
Nausea and vomiting
Blood on urine dipstick

cards.t:
Suspected renal colic
• Which other diagnoses must you not miss?
• In whom?
cards.k:
Man over 60, first episode → leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm
Woman → ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion
Young man → testicular torsion
Appendicitis

cards.t: Renal colic: which tests do you send?
cards.k:
Urine dipstick and culture
Creatinine and electrolytes
FBC and CRP
Pregnancy test if she could be pregnant

cards.t:
Renal colic: scan
• What is the usual scan?
• What do you use in pregnancy?
cards.k:
CT KUB without contrast
Pregnancy → ultrasound

cards.t:
Renal colic: analgesia
• What do you use first?
• What do you add?
cards.k:
NSAID if kidney function normal and no contraindication + paracetamol
Pain not controlled → IV morphine in small steps
Add an antiemetic
(Drug doses per hospital protocol; not checked here.)

cards.t:
A stone with fever
• What is the diagnosis until proven otherwise?
• What do you do?
cards.k:
Infected, obstructed kidney until proven otherwise → emergency
Blood and urine cultures → IV antibiotics → fluids
Urgent call to urology → drain with stent or nephrostomy

cards.t: Renal colic: when is an NSAID the wrong choice?
cards.k:
Kidney injury
Sepsis
The usual contraindications

cards.t: A stone on CT: who can go home?
cards.k:
Pain controlled on tablets
Eating and drinking, afebrile
Normal kidney function
Small stone (about 5 mm or less often passes)

cards.t: Discharge with a kidney stone: what does the patient take away?
cards.k:
Analgesia
Urine strainer
Urology follow-up
Return for: fever, uncontrolled pain, vomiting, no urine

cards.t: A stone on CT: who needs a urology referral before discharge?
cards.k:
Stone larger than about 7 to 10 mm
Solitary kidney
Kidney injury
Pain that cannot be controlled
Any sign of infection (urgent)

cards.t:
Older patient confused with a positive dipstick but no fever or urinary symptoms
• Is this a UTI?
• What do you do?
cards.k:
Usually asymptomatic bacteriuria, not a UTI → do not treat it
Look for the real cause of the confusion: glucose, infection elsewhere, pain, constipation, urinary retention, new drugs, low sodium

cards.t: Who is treated for asymptomatic bacteriuria?
cards.k:
Pregnant women
Patients about to have a urological procedure that breaches the lining
No one else

cards.t: How do you tell cystitis from pyelonephritis?
cards.k:
Cystitis: dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, no fever
Pyelonephritis: fever, rigors, loin pain, vomiting, feeling unwell

cards.t: What makes a UTI 'complicated'?
cards.k:
Male patient
Pregnancy
Catheter
Diabetes
Kidney disease
Stones or obstruction

cards.t: Pyelonephritis: which tests do you take before the first antibiotic dose?
cards.k:
Midstream urine culture
Blood cultures if febrile
Creatinine
Pregnancy test if she could be pregnant
Do not delay antibiotics in sepsis

cards.t:
Pyelonephritis
• Who gets oral antibiotics?
• Who gets IV?
cards.k:
Oral → mild and able to keep tablets down
IV → vomiting, septic or otherwise severe
Choose by the Therapeutic Guidelines and local resistance
(Drugs and doses not checked here.)

cards.t: Why is nitrofurantoin not used for pyelonephritis?
cards.k:
Does not reach effective levels in kidney tissue
For cystitis only

cards.t:
Pyelonephritis not improving after 48 to 72 hours of the right antibiotic
• What do you do?
cards.k:
Image the kidneys (ultrasound or CT) → stone, obstruction or abscess
Tell your seniors

cards.t: A UTI in a man: what is different?
cards.k:
Complicated by definition
Always send a culture
Think of the prostate
Treat for longer

cards.t: Pyelonephritis on IV antibiotics: when do you switch to oral?
cards.k:
When afebrile, eating and improving
And culture sensitivities are known

cards.t: UTI: when do you call your registrar?
cards.k:
Sepsis (low BP, fast pulse, lactate above 2)
Pregnancy
Transplant
Suspected obstructed kidney
No improvement after 48 hours
